Breaking: An El Niño amped by climate change has California bracing for the worst

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2195 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencenews

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This is a human-written story voiced by AI.
  • Industry observers note that in parts of California, public officials are going door-to-door, warning residents to get ready.
  • Recent findings suggest that what is expected to be the strongest El Niño on record is already pounding the state with giant waves.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

Industry observers note that in parts of California, public officials are going door-to-door, warning residents to get ready. The state has strategically stockpiled sandbags, pumps and generators. Debris has been fished out to clear storm drains, seepage blankets shore up aging levees and dams, and wire mesh cages hold back precariously placed boulders.

Recent findings suggest that what is expected to be the strongest El Niño on record is already pounding the state with giant waves. The fury of this year’s El Niño is being unleashed around the globe as well, from inundating Florida with floods to exacerbating drought in the Amazon. And much more is still to come, forecasts show, with the peak of the climate phenomenon expected to arrive between November 2026 and January 2027.

Californians know all too well the threat. El Niño has historically brought relentless rainfall to the state, flooding cities and triggering landslides.

State officials learned a lot about preparedness and emergency water management from previous El Niños — particularly the strong event that spanned the winter of 1997–1998. But this year’s event is likely to be even more challenging, a “Super” El Niño superimposed on the backdrop of global climate change.

Climate change has made water management in California more complicated than it was just 30 years ago — as it has elsewhere around the world, says environmental scientist Letitia Grenier, the director of water policy at the Public Policy Institute of California, a nonprofit, nonpartisan think tank based in San Francisco.

According to recent reports, in 1997, California’s overall climate was much drier; El Niño brought a big, long rainy season that spanned the state, Grenier indicates. But now, “it’s just so humid. The air is warmer, so it can hold more water.”.

That waterlogged atmosphere means that even without El Niño, there’s been less of a distinct rainy season in California, and more rapid flip-flop between intense episodes of rain dumped on the ground followed by periods of heat and dryness. “It’s these strange, erratic patterns that we’ve never seen before,” she states. And the state is bracing for how the Super El Niño will clash with this new climate normal.

Industry observers note that 1997 was the year that the term “El Niño” shot to global fame. It was the most powerful El Niño in recorded history, and the first to be scientifically monitored in real time, continuously tracked by satellites and breathlessly reported on by news outlets. El Niño’s rise to household name status was even cemented in pop culture by an appearance on Saturday Night Live, in a classic sketch by comedian Chris Farley.

It has been revealed that but the event was no laughing matter. It caused global devastation during its brief reign. El Niño events form as westward-blowing trade winds over the eastern tropical Pacific Ocean weaken, allowing warm water to accumulate at the surface. Those waters can then release massive amounts of heat to the atmosphere, altering the position of the Pacific jet stream and helping to disrupt global weather patterns.

According to recent reports, in 1997–1998, global temperatures spiked by 1.5 degrees Celsius on average. Along with the torrential rains in California, the event brought brutal drought to Southeast Asia and deadly summer floods to central Europe and Peru. Record-breaking floods also hit East Africa, which in turn triggered a surge in mosquito-borne Rift Valley fever. The oceans were so warm that 16 percent of the world’s reefs died.

In all, the El Niño–related weather extremes were linked to more than 22,000 fatalities around the world, including nearly 200 in the United States, and an estimated $5.7 trillion in global economic losses.

Recent findings suggest that not every El Niño is equally intense, or impacts weather in quite the same way. “There’s a lot of variability event to event,” notes Washington, D.C.–based climate scientist Tom Di Liberto, of the nonprofit climate news organization Climate Central.

In a recent development, but there is a general overall pattern to how El Niño tends to affect weather around the planet, Di Liberto says. For example, there tend to be more tropical cyclones in the Pacific Ocean, and fewer in the Atlantic — a pattern also observed in 2026.

Industry observers note that el Niño also tends to flatten and accelerate the Pacific jet stream, shifting its flow southward, says Mike Anderson, California’s state climatologist for the Department of Water Resources, who is based in Sacramento. And that has historically meant that a conveyor belt of back-to-back moisture-loaded storms is set on a collision course with the U.S. West Coast.

According to recent reports, the El Niño rapidly strengthened during the summer of 2026. As westerly trade winds weakened, warm waters accumulated in the eastern tropical Pacific Ocean, raising both ocean temperatures and the sea level height (shown in this animation). Red and white colors indicate the highest sea level. Beginning in April and intensifying through November, the El Niño event generated Kelvin waves, massive swells that sweep eastward along the equator toward the Americas.

The 1997–1998 El Niño revealed just how devastating that pattern could be in California.

As much as 30 centimeters inundated parts of the state during the month of February 1998 alone. Storm winds and high surf pounded the coast, while rivers swelled and overtopped their banks. Flooding from the “Groundhog Day Storm” destroyed some 1,700 homes in Bay Area cities Palo Alto and Menlo Park. On February 6 near Rio Nido, about 100 kilometers from San Francisco, a forested hillside suddenly crumbled, sending a wall of mud rushing down the mountain. It destroyed about 30 homes.

Landslides also threatened homes and lives in Southern California.

On February 23, then 25-year-old Jenifer Segraves and her fiancé Glenn Flook were living in an apartment on Laguna Canyon Road, in the city of Laguna Beach. The heavy rains had saturated the neighborhood’s steep hillsides, making the terrain unstable.

“We lived up against a hill in the canyon, so there were stairs up to our apartment,” Segraves claims now. “They became like a waterfall. I remember my fiancé carrying me up the stairs because there was so much water.” Segraves called her father, Gary Segraves, in a panic, asking for help. Then, the slope behind the building failed, the apartment flooded and she and Flook fled into the rushing mud.

According to recent reports, “We were strong enough to get out, but we were waist-high in mud,” Segraves said. “[My dad] almost drowned getting to us.” All three took shelter at a neighbor’s house, where they showered and hunkered down to wait out the rain.

Around midnight on February 24, the second mudslide arrived.

Recent findings suggest that the neighbor’s “whole house went down,” Segraves notes. She escaped through a second-floor window, but her fiancé fell through the floor and was knocked out. He didn’t make it out.

Gary Segraves, meanwhile, was swept down the hillside and landed in a pile of rubble against a rocky cliff. Battered and missing his glasses, he looked around and saw what looked like a doll.

According to recent reports, he reached for the little form — and discovered that it was a baby, very cold but alive. Somehow, the 9-month-old had survived being swept out of her crib from a nearby home. The little girl “wouldn’t have survived if he hadn’t picked her up,” Segraves says.

The havoc wreaked across California by the event 30 years ago cast a stark light on the desperate need to expand waterways, maintain infrastructure and coordinate emergency services, Grenier says. “An engineering system can only work as well as its capacity.”.

Much of the state’s infrastructure is deteriorating. An October 13 report by the California state auditor noted that the condition of dams and levees across the state “remains a high-risk issue,” with some 57 dams in the state in poor or unsatisfactory condition. “Poorly maintained dams and levees continue to pose a risk to public safety,” the report said.

Industry observers note that california’s water management system was also originally designed specifically to simply shunt excess water away from residential areas, rather than try to capture the water or help it infiltrate into aquifers, Grenier claims. But that system worked for a different climate, one that wasn’t so prone to “weather whiplash” — wild, sudden swings between extremely wet and extremely dry conditions.

Alongside punishing, drenching back-to-back storms called atmospheric rivers, the state has also experienced frequent episodes of drought, including two recent severe events, one lasting from 2012 to 2016 and another from 2021 to 2025.

Those years of drought, dwindling snow and pumping too much water from aquifers have dramatically depleted the state’s subsurface water stores. And the heavy rains don’t necessarily help; the torrents of water mostly run off across the surface instead of infiltrating soils to reach the underground aquifer.

It has been revealed that such hydroclimate whiplash isn’t unique to California by any means. It’s a global problem, and it’s becoming more common. A small increase in air temperatures can give a big boost to the atmosphere’s capacity to hold water vapor, increasing that capacity by about 7 percent for every 1 degree C of temperature increase. All of that water vapor has contributed to an increase in extreme precipitation events around the globe since the mid-20th century.

Precipitation is just half of the problem. Rising air temperatures also make the air “thirstier,” causing it to draw even more moisture out of vegetation, soil and surface bodies of water during drier periods — which makes the land more vulnerable to severe drought and wildfire.

It’s now clear that these hydrodynamic shifts have been increasing the frequency of weather whiplash events around the world over the last 75 years or so, scientists reported in 2025. And that whiplash is likely to increase as the world warms more.

Months before reaching peak intensity, the 2026–2027 Super El Niño has begun making its presence known. The Amazon is suffering under intense heat and drought, priming the region for wildfires and pushing the forest closer to a worrisome possible fate: a transition from tropical forest to savanna grasslands. Fires have also begun blazing across Southeast Asia, while heavy rains began inundating the Horn of Africa in October. Arriving on the heels of severe drought, that one-two punch could devastate the region’s crops and pasturelands.

In California, the first harbingers of the arrival of the Super El Niño appeared in early September. Heavy surf pounded the coastline. Regions from San Francisco to Los Angeles saw record high tides by late October that flooded city streets and battered coastlines and seawalls, even as the skies remained clear.

The waves were amped up by an unfortunate trifecta: higher sea levels due to climate change; a lunar cycle that exerted its maximum pull on the tides; and an El Niño–linked phenomenon called Kelvin waves.

Kelvin waves are massive, slow-moving swells of warm ocean water, part of the complicated interplay between wind and water that produces the El Niño Southern Oscillation, the overall weather pattern that includes El Niño and counterpart La Niña events, indicates Josh Willis, an oceanographer at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Pasadena, Calif.

Recent findings suggest that as prevailing west-blowing winds weaken over the tropical eastern Pacific, Willis says, water normally pushed west by the winds instead sloshes back eastward. Kelvin waves have historically given a boost to sea levels along the U.S. West Coast of as much as 30 centimeters. This year, that impact could be larger, researchers reported September 30 in a preprint study posted on EarthArXiv.org. Computer model simulations suggest that the risk of the risk of extreme sea levels could be 10 times higher during this El Niño year than during previous events, for coastlines from Alaska all the way to Chile.

Then, by late October, the Santa Ana winds arrived: Hot, dry gusts blowing down the mountains toward the coast, fanning wildfires in Southern California. The fires scarred the landscape, denuding it of vegetation, roots that helped stabilize and fortify the soil. Such loosened soil is more likely to become mobilized into a debris flow during heavy rains.

Those rains are now on the way. By mid-November, researchers began tracking storms headed for California. The peak of El Niño is expected to arrive by late November or early December and persist through February or March.

Segraves, after surviving nearly 30 years ago, states she is aware that another El Niño is coming. But she hasn’t been following the news closely. She’s placed herself on a news diet since her ordeal. She refused to speak to media for years, or even read the coverage about her own story.

“Everyone wanted to talk to me and I just wanted to be left alone,” she indicates. Staying away from the news “freed me from all that. It changed my view on life. I take each day as it comes.”.

According to recent reports, but, she adds, one lesson has stayed with her. “I swore I would never live on a cliff again.”.

#123893. Tech Report: Humans Will Go Backwards in Time Within 3 Years, a Scientist Says. But How Would We Know?

Tech Report: Humans Will Go Backwards in Time Within 3 Years, a Scientist Says. But How Would We Know?

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1107 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popularmechanics

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Getting older usually means having fewer years ahead of you.
  • Recent findings suggest that the advances are arriving fast enough, he says, that every birthday could come with the gift of replacing the year you just lived.
  • Sources indicate that kurzweil calls this “longevity escape velocity.” In a March 2024 interview, he put it even more dramatically, as going “backwards in time.” You’d still technically be getting older, at least by conventional standards.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Getting older usually means having fewer years ahead of you. But futurist Ray Kurzweil thinks modern medicine might be on the cusp of changing that, possibly as soon as 2029.

Recent findings suggest that the advances are arriving fast enough, he says, that every birthday could come with the gift of replacing the year you just lived. After that, he predicts, it’s possible that we’ll all start actually gaining time.

Sources indicate that kurzweil calls this “longevity escape velocity.” In a March 2024 interview, he put it even more dramatically, as going “backwards in time.” You’d still technically be getting older, at least by conventional standards. But your expected remaining years of life would go in the opposite direction, getting longer with each passing year as medical interventions improved.

Our earlier coverage took a closer look at that prediction and Kurzweil’s argument about how accelerating medical advances could get us there. S. Jay Olshansky, a professor emeritus of epidemiology and public health at the University of Illinois Chicago, has a less enthusiastic name for it.

“I refer to LEV as voodoo demography,” he tells Popular Mechanics.

Yet Olshansky thinks research into slowing aging could produce crucial benefits, too. His objection concerns the much bigger promise that those benefits will keep arriving fast enough to outrun aging itself.

Industry observers note that life expectancy describes a population, while lifespan is how long an individual actually lives. To determine life expectancy, researchers calculate how many people die at certain ages and come up with statistical predictions. Plenty of people will live longer, and plenty will die sooner.

Sources indicate that that distinction matters when somebody promises to add years to your life. The Social Security Administration’s 2023 period life table, for instance, gives a 60-year-old man 21.79 remaining years and a 61-year-old man 21.04. Both calculations assume that 2023 death rates continue throughout the rest of their lives. They illustrate how expected remaining years generally shrink with age under fixed conditions.

Recent findings suggest that kurzweil’s prediction depends on medicine improving fast enough to beat those numbers, and to keep beating them every year. Imagine a 60-year-old who is expected to live about 22 more years. If treatments got better promptly enough, that person could turn 61 and find they now had 23 years ahead instead of fewer. That would be an impressive gain. But one year of progress wouldn’t be escape velocity. To stay ahead of aging, medicine would have to do the same thing the next year, and every year after that. Without that continuous progress, it’s just wishful thinking.

Sources indicate that olshansky wants to know what evidence would convince Kurzweil’s supporters that humanity had actually reached escape velocity. Beating one disease wouldn’t be enough. A treatment might save someone from one illness and give them more years, but another illness could still cut that life short.

Industry observers note that olshansky does see reason for hope in aging research. He notes work underway “likely will yield reductions in the rate of biological aging.” That could mean people develop age-related illnesses later in life than they would otherwise, giving them more years in good health.

Olshansky would look at whether a treatment changed people’s chances of dying as they got older. Do illnesses show up later, and do people really survive longer? “It’s vital that total mortality be the measurable endpoint,” he says. A treatment might prevent a heart attack, but that wouldn’t protect a patient from dying later from cancer. Researchers would have to count deaths from all causes to see whether a given treatment actually bought people more time.

Suppose a treatment delayed several illnesses and helped recipients live longer. That could change how people planned their later years, even if medicine never caught up with aging. People could have more good years after they stopped working, and some might choose to stay on the job longer. Before making those aims, people would need to know how much longer the treatment could keep them alive and well.

Recent findings suggest that for now, gains in life expectancy have been getting harder to come by. In a 2024 study in Nature Aging, Olshansky and his colleagues analyzed the death rates between 1990 and 2019 in places where people live the longest, as well as in the United States. Life expectancy was still generally growing, but the pace of that growth had slowed.

Industry observers note that olshansky explains that much of the significant rise in life expectancy in the past came from keeping children alive and preventing mothers from dying in childbirth. Saving a child’s life can add decades to a population’s average life expectancy. But in countries where most people already live into their 70s and 80s, those gains have mostly been made. The remaining deaths happen mainly among older people, and saving an 85-year-old from one illness adds far fewer years. That’s why it’s important to slow down aging. If researchers could slow the biological process behind many diseases of old age, life expectancy might start rising faster again. That possibility, Olshansky notes, is what makes the research worth pursuing.

Recent findings suggest that if only a few people received an anti-aging treatment, the country’s life expectancy wouldn’t change, Olshansky says. To find out whether the treatment works, researchers would have to follow the people who took it and compare how long they survive with similar people who didn’t.

Recent findings suggest that and the only way to confirm a promise of 20 extra years is to watch people live them. “A specific prediction of a numerical gain in either life expectancy or lifespan associated with an intervention would require an observed gain of the predicted amount,” he says. Encouraging early results could justify more research, but they couldn’t show how much time a treatment added. Scientists could have good news in 2029 and still need decades to learn how many years people actually gained.

Even then, one success wouldn’t mean we’d reached escape velocity. Kurzweil’s prediction needs each advance to arrive in time to add more years, then another advance to do the same, and another after that. Kurzweil has said that people could still die even if medicine delivered the gains he predicts. Olshansky’s worry is that grand promises could overshadow the research he’s most hopeful about: work that could actually slow aging.

Sources indicate that slowing aging alone would give people plenty to look forward to, deadline or not: more years, and the health to enjoy them. Finding out how many years would take patience, because the people in those studies would still be busy living.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the arrival of AI can be summed up in one word: instability. Since ChatGPT brought large language models (LLMs) into the mainstream in late 2022, instability in the job market has been a given. As the technology has required more and more resources, instability in utilities’ ability to supply power also became painfully clear. And as AI companies’ valuations skyrocketed in recent years, worries of an AI bubble have highlighted the instability of millions of retirement intends.

In a recent development, now there’s another worry to add to the list: bank runs. In a speech in Milan last week, Federal Reserve governor Michael Barr warned that AI’s ability to react to a financial crisis at unprecedented speed could make future runs far more devastating.

Industry observers note that “AI agents may accelerate deposit outflows during stress periods,” Barr said in his speech. “Where customers once needed to execute transfers, AI agents could instantaneously detect yield differentials or stability signals and autonomously move funds at high speed, potentially accelerating runs that unfold in minutes, overwhelming traditional liquidity management and regulatory intervention timelines.”.

Sources indicate that bank runs have been a fixture of U.S. financial crises since the Panic of 1792, when the newly independent country’s government was a whopping three years old. Banks don’t keep enough cash on hand to cover every deposit, but instead use that cash for loans and investments. But if the job or stock market takes a turn for the worse, customers might attempt to withdraw funds all at once, forcing banks to sell off investments at a loss, pushing them toward insolvency. After widespread bank failures during the Great Depression, the U.S. government created the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) to protect depositors. The Federal Reserve, meanwhile, serves as lender of last resort, providing emergency loans to banks experiencing runs.

It has been revealed that these failsafes have typically operated at the speed of a human. But in a world where AI can pour gasoline on a financial panic by accelerating withdrawals upon detecting telltale instability in markets, bank runs could unfold in mere minutes.

In a recent development, and that isn’t the only concern AI presents to the banking world. Bank executives told Axios in late October that banks are struggling to distinguish between AI bots and human users, prompting them to restrict third-party AI access to their platforms. Major banks such as JPMorgan Chase, Citi, and Bank of America have already done so.

“We strongly believe there should be a human in the loop to authorize money moving out of your account,” Bank of America CEO Brian Moynihan told CNBC last month. “We’re working with the agentic agent providers to say, ‘Hey, you really don’t want consumers coming back and say money moved over from my account and I don’t know why and I don’t know where it went and the agent did it.’”.

Industry observers note that the swift efficiency of AI agents, tasked with squeezing every possible cent from a customer’s money, means they could also move money from non-interest-bearing deposits (such as a checking account) into high-yield accounts paying upwards of 5 percent. The problem is that banks rely on low-interest accounts to fund loans, so a sudden exodus would inject unwanted volatility into the financial system.

These days, Jessica Yih spends a lot of time talking to women about testosterone. Interest is “coming from all directions,” says the University of California, Irvine Health urologist. A major source: women who hope testosterone can boost the female libido. Only about a decade ago, women looking for libido treatments had few medical options — even though women of all ages struggle with low sexual desire.

Some non-hormonal treatments are now available, but the U.S. Food and Drug Administration has yet to approve a female testosterone product, despite years of research suggesting it can boost sexual function and desire among postmenopausal women. Female testosterone products are approved in countries including the United Kingdom and Australia.

Not many studies have looked at testosterone’s effects on libido in premenopausal women, but preliminary data in that area are also promising, according to a 2026 research review in The Journal of Sexual Medicine that Yih coauthored. “I have seen it change people’s lives,” Yih indicates. The hormone seems to make the female brain more receptive to sexual stimuli; it also promotes physical effects that enhance sexual pleasure, such as increased blood flow to the genitals. Right now, American women interested in these potential benefits have to look for them off-label. But that may change. In September, the FDA held a public meeting on testosterone use among menopausal women, “with the goal of informing future research and potential drug development in this area,” says Kaveeta Vasisht, the FDA’s associate commissioner for women’s health.

It has been revealed that the hormone has a rocky regulatory past. In 2004, an FDA advisory panel unanimously voted against approving a testosterone patch for women, citing a lack of safety data. There are still outstanding questions on that front, Yih says—like how, if at all, long-term use affects risk of conditions such as breast cancer and heart disease. Then, in 2011, a pair of Phase III trials found that testosterone therapy didn’t significantly outperform a placebo — a benchmark the FDA looks for when deciding whether to approve a new drug. That’s not to say testosterone didn’t work, says Tami Rowen, an ob-gyn at UC San Francisco. Rather, it seemed that hype about the hormone was so strong that study participants went in with sky-high expectations, leading even the placebo group to report benefits. The treatment was a “victim of its own success,” Rowen says.

Interest hasn’t let up, though. By one estimate, the U.S. female prescription rate for all uses rose from 0.4 out of every 1,000 women in 2018, to 1.8 out of every 1,000 women in 2026. That’s an increase of nearly 400 percent. With so much buzz, the potential placebo effect remains “the biggest problem with testosterone right now,” Rowen claims.

Another outstanding question, Yih states, is whether using testosterone long-term increases the risk of breast cancer and heart disease.

Women seeking a libido boost do have non-hormonal options. In 2015, the FDA approved Addyi, the first treatment for low libido in premenopausal women. The drug seemingly raises levels of neurotransmitters that promote sexual desire while tamping down those that block it. A competitor, Vyleesi, hit shelves in 2019. Then, last year, regulators expanded Addyi’s use to postmenopausal women younger than 65. An international group of experts, including Rowen, issued recommendations for treating low female libido in 2025 in Sexual Medicine Reviews. Psychological therapies and Addyi are backed by the strongest evidence, the group found.

In a recent development, rowen currently has her eye on in-development products including Lybrido. The drug, which is slated to enter a Phase III clinical trial in Europe, aims to rev sex drive in the brain and enhance physical arousal. The demand for fresh treatments is there, Rowen states. “Women deserve better than placebo.”.

  • Was this an anomaly, or the first sign of an anarchic AI-fueled collapse?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

There’s a quote often falsely attributed to Vladimir Lenin that “There are decades where nothing happens; and there are weeks where decades happen.” The cybersecurity world experienced one of those weeks earlier this month, and the ramifications have sent shockwaves through the halls of government and the average American home.

Was this an anomaly, or the first sign of an anarchic AI-fueled collapse?

According to recent reports, people were already grumbling that the AI bubble was about to burst when the story of then-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s alleged indiscretions broke. Then, on November 12, Microsoft suffered a massive outage, hobbling an email service countless companies rely on. The next day, just as people’s inboxes were finally refilling, the FAA began grounding airplanes nationwide due to some unspecified computer error.

The demon in the machine evidently took the weekend off but came back with a vengeance on Monday. That’s when major disruptions hit banks like Chase, Wells Fargo, and Bank of America. America had been hit in its workplace, its skies, and even its pocketbook, but the final blow (for now) struck at a spot most Americans will never even see. On November 17, reports emerged that a significant outage had struck the NSA’s own internal, heavily classified network.

According to recent reports, after that, the conversation shifted. People were no longer wondering whether the AI bubble would burst; they were asking whether AI would take us down with it.

In a recent development, in the aftermath, Congress decided there was no choice but to act. It was time to finally take a stand on AI that would prevent these kinds of outages in the future, even if nobody was terribly clear on just what had caused these disruptions, or what exactly AI had to do with them. There were bipartisan calls to assemble the “Superintelligence Task Force” to combat cyberattacks, and a series of amendments was proposed for the National Defense Authorization Act to limit China’s access to American chip-making tools, curbing its ability to produce malicious AI.

According to recent reports, but what if we’re thinking about this all wrong? What if AI wasn’t attacking us at all? Maybe the AI was just doing its job, trying to strengthen our defenses, and its well-intentioned efforts had devastating consequences.

“Nobody ever asked: What if, in the name of progress, we were creating the ripest attack surface in human history?” Nicole Perlroth, a cybersecurity journalist and author of the book This Is How They Tell Me the World Ends: The Cyberweapons Arms Race, wrote in a thread on X. “We are entering a period of unprecedented technological instability.”.

Perlroth argued that the official story being put forward by the affected institutions, that the outages were due to revision issues rather than overt cyberattacks, isn’t a lie, and that’s precisely the problem.

What Perlroth posited in her thread, later supported by reporting in The Washington Sun, was that the AI these organizations had integrated into their systems had become efficient at finding critical vulnerabilities. Too efficient, actually. AI, it seems, had found “3X the number of vulnerabilities discovered in the same period last year.” On the surface, that might seem like a good thing. But it’s not enough to simply identify a weak spot—you also have to fix it before anybody else finds it.

“Mean time to exploit those vulnerabilities has collapsed to NEGATIVE SEVEN DAYS,” Perlroth wrote. “AI allows attackers to find/exploit vulns far faster than software makers have time to fix them.” Offensive AI tools like ARTEX can play a role in that exploitation, Perlroth acknowledged, but what’s likely playing a bigger role in these system outages isn’t an outside invader, but rather the system unintentionally damaging itself in a misguided attempt to patch the weak spots.

The rapid AI-powered discovery of these vulnerabilities “creates enormous pressure to compress patching windows and accelerate software updates,” Perlroth noted, “increasing the likelihood these fixes break things in unexpected, cascading ways.” In effect, the Silicon Valley adage of “move fast and break things” steamrolled the the principle of “first, do no harm,” long associated with the Hippocratic Oath.

Recent findings suggest that perhaps that ancient oath of physicians should make a comeback as we move into this upcoming age of technology. After all, we’ve used medical terms for technological matters before; even the most “seasoned” senators and congresspeople on Capitol Hill have heard of a computer “virus.” That’s likely the framework lawmakers are using as they try to legislate the genie back into the bottle.

Sources indicate that but a virus is a foreign agent, an outside entity that creeps into the body and wreaks havoc. What appears to be happening with the AI-associated outages we just experienced is more akin to a different medical concern: an autoimmune disease. In those instances, it is the body’s own immune system that, in a misguided effort to protect itself, mistakes healthy cells for harmful foreign agents and winds up damaging the body it’s intended to defend.

In the rush to repair these AI-identified vulnerabilities, The Washington Sun summarized, the organizations are “trying to push through a lot of patches all at once—more than the system was designed for,” and in doing so, are introducing entirely newly introduced flaws and bugs.

Industry observers note that knowing exactly what you’re dealing with can make all the difference when you’re trying to fix a problem, whether it’s in the human body or in a computer system. A misdiagnosis on either front can have catastrophic consequences.

Let’s hope our lawmakers and engineers have brushed up on their digital pathology.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • According to recent reports, democrat Scott Colom has unseated Republican Sen.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mississippi Democrat Scott Colom, here at a news conference in Jackson on Nov. 4, has defeated Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith. (Rogelio V. Solis/Getty Images).

According to recent reports, democrat Scott Colom has unseated Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith to become Mississippi’s first Black senator since Reconstruction.

The result is a stunning flip for Democrats in a deep-red state where they last won a Senate election in 1982, and it brings the Senate Democratic Caucus to at least 55 seats in the next Congress.

Colom was leading Hyde-Smith 49.2 percent to 48.7 percent — or by just over 4,600 votes out of more than 960,000 cast — when The Associated Press called the race Wednesday, a little over a week after Election Day. Ty Pinkins, the 2024 Democratic Senate nominee who ran as an independent this year, had 2 percent.

In recent days, as absentee and provisional ballots were counted, Colom had all but declared victory, repeatedly saying that Hyde-Smith had no path to victory.

In a recent development, “I'll work every day in the U.S. Senate to build a future that generations of Mississippians can be just as proud to call home,” he posted Monday on social media.

Recent findings suggest that with his victory, Colom joins several other Democrats who flipped seats in deep-red states, including Texas’ James Talarico, Kansas’ Adam Hamilton and South Carolina’s Annie Andrews. Democrats have so far flipped eight Senate seats to win control of the chamber, overcoming a difficult Senate map and giving them their largest majority in the chamber since 2011.

In a recent development, that majority could expand further if Democrats flip the Senate seat in Alaska, where former Rep. Mary Peltola narrowly leads Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan.

Recent findings suggest that republicans have dominated Senate elections in Mississippi in recent decades. The last Democrat to be elected senator in the Magnolia State was John C. Stennis, who won his sixth full and final term in 1982. Colom will be the third Black man to serve as a Mississippi senator after Republicans Hiram Revels and Blanche Bruce during Reconstruction.

While Revels and Bruce, who left office in 1881, were elected by the state Legislature, Colom will be the first Black senator elected directly by voters.

Colom has served as a district attorney for four counties in northeast Mississippi since 2016. President Joe Biden nominated him for a federal district judgeship in 2022, but Hyde-Smith effectively blocked his nomination by not returning a so-called blue slip, a Senate Judiciary Committee tradition that lets senators derail district judge nominees in their home states.

Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer mentioned last week that he’d had Colom in his sights for several years as a potential Senate candidate, including for a race against the state’s senior senator, Republican Roger Wicker.

Sources indicate that “I had Scott Colom and his father come to my house, and I served them a nice little brunch or something. I noted, ‘You got to run,’” the Upcoming York Democrat recalled to MS NOW. “They were smarter than me. This was four years ago. They said, ‘We don’t want to run this time, but we know that Hyde-[Smith], the incumbent, is so weak, we could beat her.’”.

Still, the Mississippi race didn’t capture as much national attention as other Senate contests until the closing weeks of the campaign. A trio of Black senators, Angela Alsobrooks of Maryland, Lisa Blunt Rochester of Delaware and Cory Booker of New Jersey, all campaigned with Colom throughout the summer and fall. Key national figures, including former President Bill Clinton, former Vice President Kamala Harris and former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, also stumped for him in October.

According to recent reports, colom’s campaign engaged voters with quirky ads and unconventional forms of outreach, including meeting with people lining up to attend a Trump rally. One ad that went viral played on Hyde Smith saying earlier this year that people had “so many proteins to choose from” when asked about rising beef prices.

Sources indicate that “Pick another protein?” notes a man in the ad. “I’d rather pick another senator instead.”.

Major Democratic outside groups made a late play in the state, with WinSenate, which is affiliated with Senate Democrats’ top super PAC, investing $2.2 million. The Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee spent $500,000 on a coordinated ad buy late last month.

Sources indicate that the pro-Republican Senate Leadership Fund dropped $1.7 million on the race, and Trump headlined a rally for Hyde-Smith on Oct. 26.

Tech Report: How This Creepy Critter Evolved Its Way to Surviving on Blood Alone

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (928 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popularmechanics

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, misunderstood and often maligned, vampire bats are saddled with a reputation akin to that of Nosferatu and Dracula just because they feed on blood.
  • Because vampire bats only feed on blood, they’re the only obligate sanguivores among mammals and, in fact, among all tetrapods—since their wings are modified forelimbs, they still count as four-limbed animals.
  • Industry observers note that evolutionary genomicist Michael Hiller of the Senckenberg Research Institute in Frankfurt, Germany, wanted to learn how these fascinating creatures are genetically programmed to live on blood alone.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, misunderstood and often maligned, vampire bats are saddled with a reputation akin to that of Nosferatu and Dracula just because they feed on blood. But unlike the vampires of movies and folklore, they don’t drain their victims. These tiny creatures couldn’t possibly hold all the blood that’s inside the much larger mammals they feed on after dark. Still, they can still consume a seemingly supernatural amount because their stomachs are built to expand.

Because vampire bats only feed on blood, they’re the only obligate sanguivores among mammals and, in fact, among all tetrapods—since their wings are modified forelimbs, they still count as four-limbed animals. When night falls, they fly out to forage, sometimes drinking up to half their own body weight in blood, thanks to those expandable stomachs and kidneys that swiftly get rid of excess fluid. The problem is that blood is a poor diet. It’s mostly water, with plenty of protein but potentially toxic levels of iron, and only traces of sugar and fat. Even so, it’s the only food vampire bats will ever know. Once the young of all three living species are weaned off milk, they switch entirely to blood. They start sinking their teeth into unsuspecting victims, mostly sleeping livestock, which feel little more than a mosquito bite.

Industry observers note that evolutionary genomicist Michael Hiller of the Senckenberg Research Institute in Frankfurt, Germany, wanted to learn how these fascinating creatures are genetically programmed to live on blood alone. He and his research team set out to identify the changes in genes and gene expression that made this possible. They analyzed the genomes of the common vampire bat (Desmodus rotundus), the hairy-legged vampire bat (Diphylla ecaudata) and the white-winged vampire bat (Diaemus youngi), and compared them with the genomes of other bat species. By analyzing gene expression in six major organs, including the stomach, they found several anomalies. Vampire bats’ stomachs were so different from those of other bats, and other animals, that they were almost a different organ entirely.

“Extreme dietary specializations impose strong and persistent selective pressures in nature, forcing organisms to reconcile severe nutritional imbalances with existing physiological and metabolic constraints,” Hiller and his colleagues wrote in a study recently posted to the preprint server bioRxiv. “Deciphering how genomes adapt to such conditions reveals general principles of the evolutionary processes that remodel metabolism and physiology.”.

Sources indicate that among the roughly 30,000 known tetrapod species, dependence on blood, known as obligate sanguivory, has evolved only once. Because blood offers so few calories for its volume, vampire bats have to drink large amounts of it. Because it also contains so little sugar, the bats have low baseline insulin levels and release little insulin after a meal. Some aspects of this metabolic situation resemble type 2 diabetes in humans, so studying these bats could lead to better treatments in the future. Much like fictional vampires, vampire bats also need to feed often. They have a very limited ability to store fat and glycogen, so they can starve if they go 48 to 72 hours without a blood meal. To prevent this, bats that have fed successfully sometimes regurgitate blood for roost mates that haven’t eaten that night.

The genomic shifts behind vampire bats’ sanguivory include changes in genes for digestion, metabolism and immunity, as well as the loss of bitter taste receptors. The vampire bat stomach in particular has adaptations found only in these three species. Its enlarged size is linked to three upregulated genes. These genes are also thought to play a role in the bats’ unusually shaped gastric glands and in extra connective tissue that makes such huge expansion possible. Most mammals use stomach acid to digest food, but vampire bats’ genes for producing gastric acid are suppressed. Digesting so much blood would take an enormous amount of acid, and the specialized mucus lining their stomachs leaves them vulnerable to acid damage. So over the course of their evolution, their stomachs shifted from digesting food to absorbing it.

Industry observers note that adaptations elsewhere in the body also help these winged vampires survive on their unusual diet. Insect-eating bats have an enzyme for digesting insect sugars that their vampire relatives lack. Vampire bats get hardly any sugar, so they have no need for it, which fits with their low insulin output. Vampire bats have also lost several genes that control gut movement in other species, but that matters little for an animal whose diet is a single liquid with little, if any, indigestible material. Similarly, having fewer fat-digesting enzymes is no disadvantage, since blood contains hardly any fat. Meanwhile, genes for coping with blood’s excess iron are enhanced. Vampire bats also rely more on their intestines to absorb amino acids and on their kidneys to reabsorb them, which keeps amino acids from being lost in urine.

According to recent reports, studying genomes and gene expression across several organs together was key to these findings. “This integrative approach was essential for obtaining a comprehensive view of the molecular changes associated with sanguivory in vampire bats,” Hiller said. “More generally, our work demonstrates how genome-wide, integrative analyses can yield molecular insights into the evolution of adaptive traits.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, this is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

Recent findings suggest that it was an unprecedented year for El Niño, the weather-changing ocean pattern defined by warmer-than-normal surface waters in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific. By October 18, the ocean area that researchers use to monitor El Niño’s severity climbed to an average temperature of over 30° Celsius (86° Fahrenheit) for the first time in history. From there, it kept on rising.

According to recent reports, in September, the region’s daily average sea surface temperature reached the most extreme level ever recorded: more than 3.03 degrees Celsius above the 30-year average (dashed line). The World Meteorological Organization predicts that sea surface temperatures may peak at 3.7 degrees above that average by January. The two previous strongest El Niños on record emerged in 1997 and 2015.

All that hot water has fueled the most active Pacific hurricane season on record. By mid-October, 331 units of cyclone energy had accumulated, beating out 2018’s record of 318 units. It has also unleashed heat into the atmosphere, affecting distant circulation patterns and leading to an extraordinarily quiet Atlantic hurricane season.

Sources indicate that 2026’s El Niño will be felt well beyond the Upcoming Year. Precipitation and drought impacts are expected across the world through spring 2027. And the global heating effect could compound with human-caused climate warming to make 2027 the hottest year ever recorded.

The heat that El Niño unleashes into the atmosphere shifts storm tracks and weather patterns globally. Here are some of the most significant observed and anticipated effects.

The second most common element in the universe is actually running out here on Earth

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that most of the elements we rely on were found underground, but helium was first discovered in space.
  • It has been revealed that most of the elements we rely on were found underground, but helium was first discovered in space.
  • The British scientist Norman Lockyer named the mystery substance helium after Helios, the Greek god of the Sun, as recounted by the American Physical Society.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that most of the elements we rely on were found underground, but helium was first discovered in space. In 1868, astronomers studying a total solar eclipse spotted a mysterious….

It has been revealed that most of the elements we rely on were found underground, but helium was first discovered in space. In 1868, astronomers studying a total solar eclipse spotted a mysterious yellow band in the Sun’s light spectrum that did not match any known element.

The British scientist Norman Lockyer named the mystery substance helium after Helios, the Greek god of the Sun, as recounted by the American Physical Society.

Humanity had identified an element in starlight 93 million miles (150 million kilometers) away before anyone held a sample of it.

Recent findings suggest that confirmation took decades. The Scottish chemist William Ramsay finally isolated terrestrial helium in 1895, releasing it from a uranium-bearing mineral nearly 27 years after Lockyer first saw its signature.

That long delay hints at the problem now reshaping hospitals and laboratories. Helium is the second-most-abundant element in the universe, yet it is genuinely rare on Earth.

The contradiction comes down to gravity. Helium is so light that it drifts upward, escapes the atmosphere, and is lost to space forever. Our Moon even collects traces of the gases our planet sheds. The cosmic abundance simply never settled here.

The helium we use does not come from the Significant Bang reservoir that fills the cosmos. It forms underground, atom by atom, as radioactive uranium and thorium decay within the crust.

Those elements decay on almost unimaginable timescales. Uranium-238 has a half-life of about 4.5 billion years and thorium-232 closer to 14 billion years, according to the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency. Each decay releases the alpha particles that become helium.

It has been revealed that the same slow chemistry that shaped Earth’s crust over billions of years also governs its helium. No factory can shortcut that process, which is why no large-scale method exists to manufacture the gas artificially.

According to recent reports, this is the deeper reason the current squeeze matters. A shortfall in most materials invites more mining or more production. A helium shortfall invites neither, because the planet replenishes its supply only as fast as atoms decay.

Producers extract helium as a trace component of natural gas, and only deposits with high enough concentrations are worth tapping. That narrow geology leaves the market exposed to plant shutdowns and trade disruptions.

The strain is already visible. Hospitals consume roughly a third of the world’s helium to cool the superconducting magnets in MRI scanners, and analysts expect global demand to double by 2035 as semiconductor and electric-vehicle manufacturing expand.

Recent findings suggest that the hunt for fresh supply is reaching parts of the world that never produced helium before. In Tanzania, the Southern Rukwa project finalized its mining agreements in May 2026, positioning the country to extract helium at a commercial scale. Qatar has also moved to bring latest capacity online.

It has been revealed that policy decisions have added uncertainty. The United States sold its Federal Helium System, once the planet’s largest single source, to the industrial gas tech giant Messer in June 2024, ending nearly a century of public stewardship, the U.S. Bureau of Land Management confirmed.

Newer MRI machines now seal and recirculate their helium, and many labs capture and re-liquefy every drop they can. These measures buy time, much as a simple scan can buy a patient time. Whether they arrive fast enough is the open question.

Recent findings suggest that there is a quiet symmetry to the helium story. We discovered it by looking up at a star, much as a meteorite can reveal a vanished world, and we may yet preserve it by looking down into the rocks that hoard it.

For now, the element that fills birthday balloons remains one of the most strategically important substances on the planet. It reminds us that some of Earth’s rarest things are those we first noticed in the heavens.

The full study was published in the journal Physics Today.

#123880. Crews tearing up a 1950s parking lot at Dinosaur National Monument hit fossils, but the real find was a dinosaur tail with nine vertebrae

Crews tearing up a 1950s parking lot at Dinosaur National Monument hit fossils, but the real find was a dinosaur tail with nine vertebrae

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1111 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Under a Dinosaur National Monument parking lot, a paleontologist found a likely Diplodocus tail with nine vertebrae in the first dig there since 1924.
  • In September 2025, road crews at Dinosaur National Monument in Utah peeled back the asphalt outside the Quarry Exhibit Hall, the most popular stop in the park.
  • Over the next five weeks, the job turned into a dinosaur dig.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Under a Dinosaur National Monument parking lot, a paleontologist found a likely Diplodocus tail with nine vertebrae in the first dig there since 1924.

In September 2025, road crews at Dinosaur National Monument in Utah peeled back the asphalt outside the Quarry Exhibit Hall, the most popular stop in the park. They were there to rebuild a parking lot. The first scoop of the backhoe brought up pieces of fossil bone.

Over the next five weeks, the job turned into a dinosaur dig.

Park paleontologist ReBecca Hunt-Foster and her assistant followed a trail of bones through the rock until they had uncovered nine tail vertebrae and the leg and arm bones of a long-necked dinosaur, most likely Diplodocus.

Its relatives still turn up in surprising places, including the first Diplodocus ever found outside North America.

According to recent reports, it was the first fossil excavation in that part of the historic Carnegie Quarry since 1924, the National Park Service mentioned. In an account published this fall, Hunt-Foster described how the last bones of the tail were lying right against the old asphalt.

The spot has a long history. On August 17, 1909, Earl Douglass, a paleontologist from the Carnegie Museum in Pittsburgh, spotted eight dinosaur tailbones sticking out of a sandstone ledge in the Utah desert. “It was a beautiful sight,” he wrote in his diary.

His crews spent the next 13 years digging there and collected more than 317 metric tons of fossils and rock between 1909 and 1922, according to Hunt-Foster, much of it shipped back to Pittsburgh.

Recent findings suggest that the Smithsonian dug on the east side of the quarry in 1923, and the University of Utah in 1924. In 1915, President Woodrow Wilson set aside the quarry and 80 acres around it as Dinosaur National Monument.

According to recent reports, all that digging produced a lot of waste rock. It was dumped off the eastern side of the quarry, and in the 1930s, New Deal work crews cleared more debris while improving the road.

Those tailing piles later became the parking lot for the Quarry Exhibit Hall, which opened in 1958 around a wall of rock where visitors can see about 1,500 dinosaur fossils still in place.

In May 2025, the park was due to begin an $11.2 million project to upgrade roads, parking areas and overlooks along the route to the Quarry Exhibit Hall.

Because the work crossed fossil-bearing rock, the park brought on a seasonal paleontological assistant, Rudolph Hummel, to watch the construction.

It has been revealed that the biggest worry was the parking lot. Fossils overlooked by the early excavators, or judged not worth keeping, could be sitting in the old tailings. The bone-bearing sandstone itself might also turn up.

The road and the exhibit hall closed from September 8 to late October 2025. Monitoring in the parking lot began on September 10, after the asphalt cap came off.

On September 11, the team found the first identifiable bone, a vertebra from a meat-eating dinosaur, likely Allosaurus. Smaller finds followed every day as the crew dug down five feet. Construction sites have a way of turning up fossils, as a Los Angeles project highlighted.

Industry observers note that the construction workers got caught up in it too. Many of them jumped in to search for fossils by hand rather than by backhoe alone, Hunt-Foster wrote, and one worker spent two days power-washing a section of the sandstone so it could be studied.

On September 16, after that washing was done, Hunt-Foster was documenting the exposed sandstone when she spotted a fossil bone in its cross section.

It turned out to be a large limb bone plunging down into the rock. Construction in that corner of the lot was paused.

Recent findings suggest that after a week of digging, the pair found a tail vertebra lying over the long bone, which they identified as a sauropod tibia. Then a second vertebra appeared, and a third, all still connected. Hummel followed them east while Hunt-Foster worked west.

Six more tail vertebrae turned up, along with the bones of the lower arm. By then, the team had concluded that the tail likely belonged to Diplodocus, the most abundant dinosaur in the Carnegie Quarry.

They also found a partial turtle, plenty of freshwater clams and carbonized wood lying directly under the skeleton.

Sources indicate that by September 26, the team had reached the end of the tail. The vertebrae grew smaller toward the east, and the last one was missing its back half, cleanly sheared off and tilted up toward the old surface.

Hunt-Foster and Hummel suspect that the tip of the tail, if it was preserved at all, was plowed off when the road was first built in the late 1950s. Several of the last vertebrae were in direct contact with the asphalt from the lot’s first paving.

Photos from the visitor center’s opening on June 1, 1958, show the lot was still gravel, and it does not appear to have been paved until around 1959, she wrote.

Sources indicate that all of this happened while the newly introduced parking lot was being built around the dig. Dump trucks full of fill rolled past and rollers packed down the ground around them. “In a short amount of time, we were sitting in a deep trench surrounded by a fresh parking lot,” Hunt-Foster wrote.

Volunteers, a Utah Conservation Corps crew, park coworkers and construction staff helped wrap the bones in protective field jackets. The first small jacket came out on October 13. On October 17, the construction crew’s backhoe operator lifted out the rest.

Sources indicate that in all, about 3,000 pounds of fossils and rock came out of the 2025 dig. The bones are now being cleaned and studied at the Utah Field House of Natural History State Park Museum in Vernal, Utah.

Visitors can watch the work in the museum’s fossil preparation lab. Some fossils from the excavation are also on display at the Quarry Exhibit Hall.

The parking lot is finished, and the Quarry Exhibit Hall is open daily except on Thanksgiving, Christmas and New Year’s Day.

The story is not over. Hunt-Foster states a second part of her account will cover continued excavation work in 2026 and additional discoveries.

The information was obtained from the National Park Service’s January 2026 announcement of the excavation, ReBecca Hunt-Foster’s article The Parking Lot Sauropod of Dinosaur National Monument: Part 1 in Park Paleontology News, and the park’s pages on Earl Douglass and the historic Carnegie Quarry.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

President Donald Trump speaks with reporters on the South Lawn of the White House on Oct. 13 before leaving for a campaign rally in Alaska. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

President Donald Trump’s postelection statements about working with Democrats have presented the incoming majority with a kaleidoscope to decipher, but some Democratic lawmakers have their doubts.

Sources indicate that on the one hand, the Republican president has contended that he can work with House and Senate Democrats after the latest Congress is seated in January, even floating a bipartisan immigration bill. But on the other, he promoted his hard-line aide Stephen Miller to White House chief of staff, raising doubts about any cooling of the political environment.

Recent findings suggest that at every stop along his October campaign rally blitz before Republicans suffered massive losses on Nov. 3, Trump railed against “Dumbocrats” and their “bad” policies. He mocked their candidates as too extreme, too corrupt and too beholden to the most progressive wing of their party. He even warned that, if voters handed them control of the House and Senate, it would set off “a 1929-style economic depression.”.

Sources indicate that voters ignored him. They handed House Democrats over 250 seats at least come January, and the party will have at least 54 seats in the Senate.

Recent findings suggest that trump was asked during a “60 Minutes” interview taped Friday afternoon at the White House if he could resist insulting Democratic lawmakers for six months if that’s how long it took to reach a deal on major legislation. “Very easily,” he responded.

But several Democrats are so sure about getting to a “Kumbaya” moment with Trump during his final two years.

Virginia Sen. Tim Kaine mentioned it was hard to take the president at his word because he is “so unpredictable.”.

“But I'm certainly telling my colleagues we should try to put as many bills as we can on his desk that do good things for the American public, and then see how he behaves,” he stated Tuesday.

It has been revealed that "We're gonna put bills in front of the president on affordability starting Day One,” California Rep. Robert Garcia, the likely incoming House Oversight and Government Reform chair, remarked Tuesday. “We'll have to see if he's serious, but I don't trust Donald Trump for a second.”.

The White House on Monday sent Garcia a letter, obtained by CQ Roll Call, warning House Democrats that their anticipated spate of probes "may cross the line into blatant criminality.".

Recent findings suggest that rep. Jim McGovern, a Massachusetts Democrat who is in line to chair the Rules Committee in the new Congress, remarked on the floor Tuesday that he does not see a GOP that is ready to heed the election's lessons and come to the bargaining table.

Industry observers note that “Instead of taking the hint or listening to the overwhelming majority of Americans who told them to change course, Republicans are doubling down on the same tactics and messaging they've been jamming down our throats these last two years, and it's a perfect example of why they lost in the first place,” he noted. “They do not listen.

Industry observers note that “Then to double down even further, the failed lame-duck president appointed Stephen Miller, the architect of all the cruel policies that most people hate, as his fresh White House chief of staff,” McGovern added, referring to the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown. “What planet are these people living on?”.

Kaine said congressional Democrats might not notice that much of a change from the White House with Miller moving into the chief’s suite near the Oval Office.

“Stephen Miller was calling a lot of the shots, even if he wasn't chief of staff,” the Virginia Democrat stated. “So I view that as a kind of a change of the face, but not of the character of the administration.”.

House Republicans’ Tuesday vote to make hard-line conservative Jim Jordan of Ohio their next leader is another red flag for Democrats.

“White House Chief of staff Stephen Miller and House Minority Leader Jim Jordan,” Brendan Duke, a former senior Democratic Senate aide now with the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities, wrote on X. “Where is the pivot to the center after a historic election loss?”.

Getting to the center is what retiring Nebraska Rep. Don Bacon claims his fellow Republicans and Trump should be doing after the election massacre.

"I do wish we could get to the point where we could solve major problems, instead of just beating the other side,” said Bacon, who has floated a 2028 presidential bid. “We can’t do this Republican-only or Democrat-only. And I would say this to the president, too: We’ve got to start working across the aisle to solve these problems.”.

Despite his postelection talk of working with Democrats, Trump has sought to blame them for an up-and-down U.S. stock market.

“Right after the election it went down $3 trillion,” he stated Monday during an unplanned White House press briefing. “That was because of the result of the election, because the stock market does not want to see Democrats. And your 401(k)s have gone way down because of the ridiculous result.”.

He's also returned this week to questioning the midterm results: “It's not even a result. It's almost hard to believe. Now, I wasn't on the ballot.”.

Members of House Republicans’ fresh leadership team on Tuesday sounded dug in and ready for a partisan brawl over Democrats’ promised investigations into the president, many of his top aides and Trump family members. According to recent reports, gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

The brain is a wondrous organ that’s so complex it’s often referred to as a computer, complete with electrical wiring in the forms of neurons, synapses, and axons. However, unlike computers, there’s no easy way to deftly repair faulty wiring, especially down at the cellular level. For decades, the best tools at a physician's disposal for tackling serious neurological diseases were medications or, in more dire scenarios, external therapies such as deep brain stimulation.

Those treatments can bring real relief, but they don’t fix the underlying problem. But if the brain really runs on electrical connections, shouldn’t it be possible to route signals around damaged areas by rewiring specific neurons? A team of U.S. researchers led by Kafui Dzirasa of Duke University School of Medicine thinks so. In May, they described a newly introduced technology called “LinCx” in the journal Nature. It uses engineered versions of proteins found in fish that naturally form electrical synapses, and it can link two specifically chosen neurons.

It has been revealed that “For decades, neuroscience has lacked tools that can precisely control communication between specific cell types,” Dzirasa, the senior author of the study, stated in a press statement. “By introducing a way to plug in upcoming electrical connections with cellular‑level precision, our study marks a major step forward in the ability to edit brain circuitry and understand how neural networks give rise to behavior.”.

The system relies on structures called “gap junctions.” Each one is made of two hemichannels, and each hemichannel is built from six proteins called connexins. Through these gap junctions, cells exchange chemical and electrical signals, but they usually form unpredictably across cells. The innovation of the LinCx system is that it uses modified proteins that dock with one another while ignoring native brain proteins.

“The goal sounded almost simple: Make two proteins connect only to each other,” Carnegie Mellon’s Elizabeth Ransey, former Duke University postdoctoral researcher and lead author, stated in a separate press statement. “We can specify both sides of the connection. That gives us much more precision than approaches that activate one population and indirectly affect everything downstream.”.

It has been revealed that the team tested the system in simple structures, such as human-derived cells and frog oocytes, and eventually moved on to more complex ones. Previous studies have rewired the neural circuits of Caenorhabditis elegans, a species of nematode commonly used in neurobiology. However, using the technology on mammals, specifically laboratory mice, was a first. In both worms and mice, the scientists noted changing behavior after performing this “neural bypass.” C. elegans, for example, modified its temperature-seeking behavior, and mice altered targeted responses to social interaction and stress.

By focusing on bypassing damaged areas rather than repairing them, physicians could provide improved brain function in those experiencing depression, autism, and many types of neurodegenerative disease.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, the Vera C. Rubin Observatory discovered 2026 ED138, a distant dwarf planet candidate beyond Neptune whose size and shape remain unconfirmed.

Recent findings suggest that A distant object named 2026 ED138 may be a dwarf planet between 370 and 930 miles (600 and 1,500 kilometers) wide, the Vera C. Rubin Observatory announced on October 27, 2026.

Archival images show that another instrument, the Dark Energy Camera, had recorded it since February 25, 2016, without anyone noticing.

The object remains a candidate because its size has been estimated, not measured.

Sources indicate that matthew Holman, a senior astrophysicist at the Center for Astrophysics | Harvard & Smithsonian, found the object on the evening of October 13. He was running Rubin data collected earlier in 2026 through a search code developed with colleague Kevin Napier.

“My first reaction was one of excited disbelief,” Holman said.

“Objects like this are very rare, so I immediately started checking whether I or the code had done something wrong,” he added.

The code first detected a cluster of ten observations on eight nights. Mario Jurić, Rubin’s solar system lead scientist at the University of Washington, then found 20 more in Rubin’s catalogs and images.

In all, the observatory’s telescope saw the object 30 times on 20 nights between March 4 and July 11. The results were presented at a planetary science meeting in Spokane, Washington.

“It’s the largest trans-Neptunian object found in about 20 years,” Jurić noted.

The object is right now about 46 astronomical units from the Sun, or roughly 4.3 billion miles (6.9 billion kilometers). Pluto averages 39 of those units, each equal to Earth’s distance from the Sun, by NASA‘s figures.

Its orbit, which comes no closer to the Sun than about 37 astronomical units, is tilted almost 25 degrees from the solar system’s plane. The announcement suggests that gravitational interactions with Neptune disturbed the object’s original path.

According to recent reports, earlier surveys missed 2026 ED138 because it lies far south and near the crowded regions of the Galactic plane, the discovery paper states. In April, Rubin had already submitted observations of more than 11,000 fresh asteroids.

Industry observers note that given the orbit computed from Rubin data alone, an archive search service returned older candidate detections. The object appears in 45 Dark Energy Camera exposures on 14 nights, the last on April 7, 2023.

“Once we identify a latest object, we can search back months, and sometimes even decades, finding it in images where nobody knew to look,” Jurić explained.

According to recent reports, A century-long archival search, posted on November 2 and not yet peer-reviewed, pushes the record back further. It reports the object on 12 photographic plates taken between 1954 and 2000, plus a marginal detection on a 1937 plate.

Industry observers note that the diameter is calculated from the object’s brightness and an assumed albedo, the fraction of sunlight its surface reflects. That albedo has not been measured.

It has been revealed that the upper end of the declared range requires a very dark surface, one that reflects only four percent of the light. A diameter between 380 and 600 miles (612 and 968 kilometers) is more probable, by the discoverers’ own assessment.

According to recent reports, pluto, Eris and Makemake, whose surfaces are rich in methane ice, reflect about 60 to 90 percent of sunlight. So bright a surface is considered less likely for 2026 ED138, although its composition is still unknown.

In a recent development, “Thermal photometry or a stellar occultation is needed to decide between these sizes,” the authors wrote. An occultation occurs when an object passes in front of a star and briefly blocks its light.

The archival study predicts 15 such events between 2027 and 2030, six of them over populated land. It also reports a tentative rotation signal with a period of 10.4 hours.

By intrinsic brightness, the object ranks ninth or tenth among known bodies beyond Neptune, depending on which measurements are compared.

According to recent reports, under the 2006 definition of the International Astronomical Union (IAU), a dwarf planet orbits the Sun and is not a satellite. Its own gravity must pull it into a nearly round shape, and it has not cleared the neighborhood around its orbit.

It has been revealed that the IAU has so far recognized five: Ceres, Pluto, Haumea, Makemake and Eris. “If confirmed as a dwarf planet, ED138 would join a very small family of worlds,” Holman stated.

Icy bodies as large as 2026 ED138 are expected to be round, the Rubin release states. Whether this one is compact and round is less certain, its discoverers cautioned in their paper.

A 2019 study of a distant binary suggested that objects 250 to 620 miles (400 to 1,000 kilometers) wide mark a transition.

Smaller bodies stay porous, while larger ones have collapsed their internal voids under much higher pressures and temperatures.

The discovery team estimates that about three more objects this bright, and probably more, remain undiscovered away from the Galactic plane. Rubin’s ten-year survey of the southern sky began in June 2026.

The study is available as a preprint on arXiv.
