💡 Key Takeaways
  • Here’s what you’ll learn when you read this story:.
  • Earlier this year, Jayne Hyde-Dryden was walking down a busy sidewalk along a noisy, two-lane road with her friend when she realized just how much her perception had changed.
  • This amazed her friend because Hyde-Dryden is blind.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Here’s what you’ll learn when you read this story:.

Earlier this year, Jayne Hyde-Dryden was walking down a busy sidewalk along a noisy, two-lane road with her friend when she realized just how much her perception had changed. Mid-conversation, her friend interrupted and noted, “Oh, that was fascinating. You just avoided a van without realizing you’d done it.”.

This amazed her friend because Hyde-Dryden is blind. She had used echolocation to detect the van, which was parked on the sidewalk, and navigated around it without even noticing. “I wasn’t consciously thinking about what I was doing at the time. Instead, I was naturally using echolocation, picking up changes in the way sound reflected from the vehicle and using that information to navigate around the obstacle,” says Hyde-Dryden, a rehabilitation teacher in the UK. Like many blind echolocators, she creates a sharp, quick sound by clicking her tongue and then listens for the echo.

While echolocation comes easily to her now, Hyde-Dryden had to work hard to learn it. Almost 20 years ago, while she was losing her sight to glaucoma, she attended a short workshop and spent hours practicing the clicking technique she learned there. But she didn’t feel confident using it until 2019 when she signed up for an intensive echolocation study at Durham University.

That study was spearheaded by Lore Thaler, PhD, a neuroscientist at Durham University whose work over the last 15 years has uncovered how echolocation changes the brain. Her research goes beyond studying the variability of perception between people, and highlights just how much one person’s perceptual reality can change, even in a short timeframe.

Thaler started her research journey studying visual perception, but her work took an unexpected turn when a collaborator introduced her to a blind echolocator. At the time, she hadn’t heard of human echolocation, but “the way he described the world was very easy to relate to from a sighted person’s perspective,” she claims.

After diving into the literature, Thaler found scattered and disjointed research on echolocation, and “very little was known about the brain basis of it,” she says. “That’s where we came in.”.

She and her collaborators used functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) to track two blind participants’ brain activity while they listened to recordings of their own echolocation clicks and echoes.

The auditory cortex responded more to echoes than non-echoes in both participants but so did regions of their visual cortex, including areas associated with visual shape perception. Even though this was what she had hoped to find, actually seeing it “was a wonderful surprise,” indicates Thaler, leading to “a great feeling of discovery.” When she and her team submitted the paper in 2011, the findings were contentious—so contentious that the journal they submitted to asked double the typical number of reviewers to take a look at it. Some thought it was an incredible finding; others thought it was predictable. But in the end, the paper got published, and when it did, it made a huge splash in the neuroscience community.

The project shifted the way Thaler’s collaborators, and later many in the field, thought about the visual cortex. Perhaps the “visual cortex” was a misleading term, some experts thought. Instead, “maybe it’s a thing for processing spatial information,” says Melvyn Goodale, PhD, a neuroscientist at Western University and Thaler’s collaborator on the project.

In a recent development, after that first study on echolocation, Thaler was hooked. She launched an entire lab of her own at Durham University dedicated to human echolocation research. She went on to study how echolocators perceive motion, navigate new spaces, and distinguish between textures like velvet or glass.

By the time Hyde-Dryden made her way to Durham in 2019, Thaler was embarking on her most ambitious project yet: a 10-week echolocation training program for both blind and sighted people.

According to recent reports, each two-hour training session involved a slew of tasks. One involved standing in front of two foam discs and deciding which was larger. Another required participants to navigate through a virtual maze with recorded clicks and echoes. During every session, participants also explored an indoor or outdoor space with the help of Thaler or one of her collaborators to practice echolocating in the real world. Thaler even brought Hyde-Dryden to the Newcastle train station to help her learn the intricacies of echolocating in a busy, loud environment. Over time, Hyde-Dryden built up a mental “library of echo patterns” for familiar objects.

In a recent development, both blind and sighted participants improved substantially at each of these tasks over the course of the 10 weeks. Just as in the initial 2011 paper and many of her follow-up studies, Thaler also wanted to understand brain activity during echolocation. This time, she had participants hop in the MRI machine both before and after learning to echolocate.

It has been revealed that before the study, Hyde-Dryden had heard from an expert blind echolocator that being inside of the MRI would feel tight and uncomfortable, but when she went into the MRI before the echolocation training, it didn’t bother her at all. After the training, however, the MRI felt quite different. “When I went in at the end, I felt horrendous. I felt ill afterwards. I felt really sick. And I think it was because I was more aware.”.

Those fMRI scans revealed that participants’ brains became attuned to echoes, whether or not they were blind. Echoes elicited a larger response in both the auditory cortex and in the primary visual cortex.

According to recent reports, “It paired I think nicely with what we, up to that point, had only been able to show in these expert echolocators,” Thaler claims. But it pushed the findings even further, demonstrating that participants don’t need to be blind to have malleable visual cortices. After just 10 weeks of training, the visual cortex becomes attuned to sounds that carry information about space. And other labs have shown that sighted people don’t even need to learn echolocation to retrain their visual cortex; a few days with a blindfold can tune your visual cortex to sound and touch signals it wouldn’t normally process.

Since that training, Hyde-Dryden has started to use echolocation every day. “It really was an absolute game changer for me,” she indicates. Thanks to echolocation, when her daughter was young, Hyde-Dryden was able to use both hands to scoop her up from the bath, bringing her into the bedroom without having to hold a cane at the same time. In conjunction with her cane and guide dog, echolocation has made Hyde-Dryden feel much more confident navigating new spaces. Even in busy train stations with high ceilings where the echo can get lost, she can find her way without assistance.

Despite success stories like hers, “it’s not a skill that is widely taught anywhere in the world,” Hyde-Dryden says. Echolocation is taught by a small number of people and is sometimes loosely included in rehabilitation curricula, “but it is certainly not given the emphasis that it should.”.

Industry observers note that thaler hopes to change that. She has offered free workshops for years and, this year, she looks to give training sessions to more than 100 rehabilitation professionals at Guide Dogs UK who will then train their hundreds of clients.

It has been revealed that “I think the neuroscience stuff has been a good vehicle to drive home the message ‘this is real, this has to be taken seriously,’” indicates Thaler. “But then to actually go out and do the training and make it useful for people, of course, that’s still another step.”.

Industry News: Most of the world’s lost glacier ice comes from a tiny minority of glaciers

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1102 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A census of 216,502 glaciers finds the 3 percent that end in lakes, seas or ice shelves drive most glacier ice loss, and lakes speed it up most.
  • In a recent development, outside of Earth’s two massive ice sheets, there are roughly 216,500 glaciers, and 97 percent of them end on bare rock.
  • Recent findings suggest that the other 3 percent end in a lake, the ocean, or a floating ice shelf.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A census of 216,502 glaciers finds the 3 percent that end in lakes, seas or ice shelves drive most glacier ice loss, and lakes speed it up most.

In a recent development, outside of Earth’s two massive ice sheets, there are roughly 216,500 glaciers, and 97 percent of them end on bare rock. Surprisingly, however, these land-based glaciers are not where most of the world’s melting ice is coming from.

Recent findings suggest that the other 3 percent end in a lake, the ocean, or a floating ice shelf. They are the ones shedding more than half of all the glacier ice lost between 2000 and 2019.

Industry observers note that those numbers come from a latest global census of where glaciers end. Glaciers that end in lakes stood out most. Relative to their size, they lost ice about 57 percent faster than glaciers ending on land. The researchers don’t yet know why.

Joe Mallalieu did the work at the University of Birmingham and is now at the University of Leeds, with Nicholas Barrand of Birmingham among the co-authors.

In an interview with Earth.com, Mallalieu said the lake result was a surprise.

“What surprised us most was how much faster glaciers ending in lakes lose ice than those ending in the ocean, relative to their size,” he said.

The team classified all 216,502 glaciers in a standard global inventory by what their fronts touch: land, a lake, the sea, or an ice shelf.

In a recent development, earlier inventories had flagged lake-ending glaciers in only three of the world’s 19 glacier regions. The team found the rest by matching glacier outlines against a satellite map of glacial lakes built from more than 250,000 Landsat scenes.

It has been revealed that then they combined that classification with existing global records of each glacier’s size, ice thickness, slope, flow speed and ice loss, plus the local climate. The full classification is public on Zenodo.

Lake-ending glaciers turned up in every one of the 19 regions. In Iceland, 65 percent of the glacier area drains to a lake, and in the southern Andes almost 40 percent does. Glaciers ending in the sea cluster in the Arctic and around Antarctica.

Glaciers that end in lakes or the sea tend to be far bigger than those ending on land. The typical lake-ending glacier covered about eight times the area of a typical land-ending one.

It was also roughly twice as thick, about 200 feet (61 meters) against 100 feet (31 meters).

Size alone explained a lot of the ice loss but not all of it. For its size, the typical lake-ending glacier lost ice equal to a layer of water about 1.6 feet (0.49 meters) deep each year.

That is roughly double the rate at land-ending and ocean-ending glaciers.

After the team accounted for climate, elevation, slope, thickness and other factors, the gap held. Lake-ending glaciers lost about 57 percent more ice for their size than land-ending ones, and they flowed about 10 percent faster.

Ocean-ending glaciers flowed 44 percent faster than land-ending ones, yet their ice loss for their size was no higher, the authors wrote.

Industry observers note that lake water can remove ice from a glacier’s front in several ways. It melts the ice below the waterline, and the undercut front breaks off as icebergs.

It can also lift the front until it floats and breaks, or seep beneath the ice and reduce the friction holding it back.

Any of those would remove ice faster than melting on bare rock does. But the lake-ending glaciers in the census were also larger and flatter at their lower ends than land-ending ones.

That shape alone can slow a glacier’s adjustment to warming and keep it losing ice for longer, the authors wrote.

Mallalieu told Earth.com that even the climate difference doesn’t account for it. “And it’s not just because they tend to be in warmer, wetter places: the difference holds even when we take climate into account,” he said.

Barrand stated the census only became possible recently. “The last decade has seen a huge increase in the global glacier and climate data available to researchers. Bringing these datasets together lets us compare how glaciers in different settings are behaving,” he said.

The categories themselves are moving. Glacial lakes grew by more than 50 percent in number and area between 1990 and 2018, according to a satellite survey in Nature Climate Change.

Sources indicate that many glaciers that once ended on land now end in water. Across the Arctic, meanwhile, glaciers that reached the sea are retreating onto land.

Asked by Earth.com what happens to those glaciers next, Mallalieu said the two switches should have opposite effects.

In a recent development, glaciers pulling back onto land are likely to slow down markedly. Glaciers newly ending in lakes are likely to speed up slightly and lose ice much faster for their size.

In the long run, he remarked, many lake-ending glaciers will retreat out of their lakes and end on land again. That matters for the models that project sea level rise and river flow.

According to recent reports, many of them don’t yet represent what happens where a glacier meets a lake, the authors wrote. Yet the glaciers that can respond this way hold more than half of the world’s glacier area.

The classification counts a glacier as lake-ending if any lake touches its front, however small the contact.

Glaciers with only a sliver of lake may behave more like land-ending ones, so the authors mentioned the real gap between the two groups is probably larger than 57 percent.

Flow speeds were available for 84 percent of glaciers and ice-loss rates for 94 percent. Furthermore, the lake map left out Svalbard and Antarctica.

Cause is also unproven: the study demonstrates lake-ending glaciers lose ice faster, not whether the lakes themselves are responsible.

For communities downstream, the open question is water. Mallalieu noted the census did not assess water supplies. But in the Himalaya, where large populations rely on meltwater, glacier lakes are expanding fast, he said.

Better models of these glaciers would give those communities more reliable forecasts of their future water.

Untangling the lakes from the glacier shapes is the next task. It means measuring individual lakes, their depth, temperature and how long they persist, glacier by glacier.

Until that is done, the 57 percent is a difference the world can see and not yet explain.

The full study was published in the journal Nature Communications.

  • For a grid that leans on wind turbines, the problem is also too little.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Climate models project that extreme heat and weak winds will coincide more often, straining power grids as cooling demand rises and wind power drops.

A heat wave feels like a problem of too much: too much sun, too much demand for air conditioning.

For a grid that leans on wind turbines, the problem is also too little.

When extreme heat coincides with unusually weak winds, wind farms can generate less electricity just as demand for air conditioning rises.

A new analysis of 27 climate models projects that these spells of extreme heat and weak winds will become two to eight and a half times more frequent over the world’s land by 2100.

How much more depends on how much carbon dioxide is emitted.

The models also project that the longest such spell each year could last roughly two to four times as long.

Lu Shen and colleagues at Peking University in Beijing led the work, with Meng Qu as first author.

The results are model projections, not measurements, and the range reflects both the emissions path and real disagreement among the models.

The team defined a bad day by two thresholds. The wind at 33 feet (10 meters) had to fall into the slowest 5% of warm-season days while the temperature rose into the hottest 5%.

If heat and calm were unrelated, such days would be rare by chance alone. They aren’t unrelated.

Across the middle and high latitudes, hotter days tend to be calmer.

In parts of the northern high latitudes, Southeast Asia and northern Africa, the two coincided five to eight times more often than chance would predict in a NASA weather record.

It has been revealed that from 1980 to 2014, the average patch of land saw about 0.6 such days a year. Russia, the southeastern coasts of the United States and China, and parts of the tropics saw 1.5 to 3 days.

Along the storm tracks between 35 and 65 degrees north, the longest spells ran more than five days.

A spell that long means most of a week of weak wind in the middle of a heat wave, in some of the most densely populated regions on Earth.

Europe’s summer of 2022 is the authors’ example. Persistent heat and weak winds coincided with surging electricity demand and rising prices.

The projections come from a NASA dataset that sharpens 27 global climate models to a grid of about 15 miles (25 kilometers).

Each model was scored against its own 1980 to 2014 climate, so the thresholds for “hot” and “calm” shift with the model rather than with the real world.

The models project more days of extreme heat and unusually weak winds by 2100, with the largest increase under the highest-emissions pathway.

Under the lowest pathway, the rise levels off after mid-century.

Industry observers note that the tropics change fastest. Between 30 degrees south and 30 degrees north, the frequency rises by 188% under the lowest pathway and by 934% under the highest. The northern mid-latitudes rise by 106% and 689%.

Sources indicate that the spells get longer as well as more common. By 2100, the models project that the longest such spell each year could last 84% to 315% longer worldwide, depending on the emissions pathway.

In a recent development, the team split the increase into four causes: hotter average temperatures, slower average winds, bigger swings in both, and a tighter link between heat and calm. Warming alone accounted for most of the rise in every latitude band.

According to recent reports, winds change differently by region. Between 30 and 60 degrees north, average winds slow by up to 0.07 miles per hour (0.03 meters per second) a decade.

The authors tie that stilling to the Arctic warming faster than the tropics, which flattens the temperature difference that drives wind.

In the tropics, winds pick up slightly, which offsets part of the warming effect.

In a recent development, the jet stream matters too. The models shift the northern jet about 1.6 degrees poleward by 2100. North of roughly 50 degrees, that shift strengthens the pairing of hot days with calm ones, and south of it the pairing weakens.

Sources indicate that twenty-seven models disagree, sometimes widely. To shrink the spread, the team checked which models best reproduced the observed trend in these compound events from 1980 to 2014.

Eight reanalysis datasets supplied the observed trend, and the projections were weighted accordingly.

The correction trimmed the projected global increase by 10% to 25% and cut the disagreement among models by 13% to 24%. The models that track history best now carry more weight, and the forecast tightens.

At the regional level it cut disagreement by 10% to 40%, raising projections for South Asia and Eastern Europe and lowering them for Southeast Asia and Latest Zealand.

The analysis uses daily averages, and the authors note that averaging smooths away the calmest hours, so the study likely undercounts the most extreme lulls.

The models also underestimate how tightly heat and calm are coupled in the northern high latitudes, which is where the events are most pronounced.

According to recent reports, the stakes the authors describe are already visible. In the eastern United States, the PJM grid hit a peak load of 162.7 gigawatts during the July 2026 heat wave, close to its summer record.

India set a demand record of 270.73 gigawatts in May 2026, with outages in places. Europe’s June 2026 heat wave was linked to more than 10,000 excess deaths.

Recent findings suggest that the authors flag the hours after sunset. Solar output disappears while demand stays high, and nights are expected to warm faster than days. European minimums already exceed 68°F (20°C) on so-called tropical nights.

The authors’ answer is long-duration storage to carry daytime solar power into those evenings, more mixing of renewable sources, and above all a lower emissions path.

In their projections, the odds of a spell of extreme heat and weak winds by 2100 are four to eight times higher under the higher-emissions pathways than under the lowest one.

What the models can’t yet say is how often the calmest hours, rather than the calmest days, will coincide with the hottest ones.

Answering that would take hourly projections the downscaled dataset doesn’t provide.

The full study was published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

Deadline looms for post-9/11 FirstNet reauthorization

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (970 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, in an aerial view, a fire truck sits parked in a neighborhood destroyed by a wildfire on Aug.
  • Supporters of the FirstNet program that provides emergency communications for first-responders still see hope for reauthorization this year, despite continued disagreements over what changes, if any, should be made to how the program is governed.
  • A House-passed reauthorization bill would shift authority toward the Commerce Department’s National Telecommunications and Information Administration and away from the FirstNet board, which is made up in part by first-responders.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, in an aerial view, a fire truck sits parked in a neighborhood destroyed by a wildfire on Aug. 11, 2023 in Lahaina, Hawaii. The performance of the FirstNet network during the Maui fires has partially led to calls for a revamp of its structure. (Justin Sullivan/Getty Images).

Supporters of the FirstNet program that provides emergency communications for first-responders still see hope for reauthorization this year, despite continued disagreements over what changes, if any, should be made to how the program is governed.

A House-passed reauthorization bill would shift authority toward the Commerce Department’s National Telecommunications and Information Administration and away from the FirstNet board, which is made up in part by first-responders.

The potential change is opposed by the influential Fraternal Order of Police, but any new bill or amendment would require floor votes in both the House and Senate, a potentially tall order as the 119th Congress draws to a close.

Authority for FirstNet, a program developed in the wake of 9/11, is set to expire in February of 2027 unless lawmakers pass an extension.

The program’s governing entity, the First Responder Network Authority, was created in 2012 in response to recommendations after the terrorist attacks, during which public safety agencies using different radio systems and overloaded phone lines struggled to adequately communicate.

In a recent development, the House passed its bipartisan reauthorization bill in April via voice vote. Senators have not yet taken up that legislation or introduced their own. In January, the Senate Commerce Committee’s Telecommunications and Media Subcommittee held a hearing on the program.

Related: First-responder network reauthorization advances.

Craig Wheeler, a spokesman for subcommittee Chair Deb Fischer, R-Neb., remarked in a statement this week that reauthorization is still a priority.

“Sen. Fischer has been working closely with Chair Cruz on a bill and is having bipartisan discussions with Ranking Member Cantwell,” Wheeler said, referring to Sens. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, and Maria Cantwell, D-Wash.

Sources indicate that “Moving a bill as soon as possible remains a top priority for Sen. Fischer, including getting it through both chambers and signed into law by President Trump.”.

The House bill would extend authority for FirstNet through fiscal 2037, stagger terms on the authority’s board and require five members of the board with public safety backgrounds, rather than three as needed under current law.

At concern in the reauthorization debate, in part, is control of the First Responder Network Authority.

The House bill would eliminate language in current law that established FirstNet as an “independent” authority within the Commerce Department’s National Telecommunications and Information Administration and would require the administration’s approval for most non-planning or emergency actions, though the bill was amended to include a list of actions the network can take without NTIA approval.

The changes are meant to respond to reports from the Commerce Department's Office of Inspector General that found that the AT&T-run service was not sufficiently available during the Maui wildfires in 2023 and that senior officials of the FirstNet Authority attempted to interfere with audits.

Sources indicate that the Maui report noted the small number of FirstNet subscriptions among state and local first responders in the area and in an op-ed earlier this year, Maui Fire Chief Brad Ventura said his department was “not using FirstNet devices” at the time of the fires but is now adopting them. He also supported reauthorization in the op-ed.

Related: First-responders network faced with calls for change.

But the shifting of control drew opposition from the Fraternal Order of Police, which prior to the bill’s committee markup urged its members to instead support a “clean reauthorization” of the program.

Sources indicate that jim Pasco, executive director of the FOP, emphasized his group’s desire to see decisions made by the FirstNet board, rather than by NTIA. He mentioned that moving authority away from a group that is required to include first-responders would be “a threat to officer and public safety.”.

Yucel Ors, legislative director for public safety and crime prevention at the National League of Cities, mentioned that his group, along with the International Association of Fire Chiefs and other state and local government and public safety groups, worked closely with the House, including on the changes to put some “everyday controls and functions” back directly under the board’s control.

He said the National League of Cities supported the House bill, but that they hope that any changes made to FirstNet’s governance are “not going to impact the day-to-day operations that public safety depend on, rely on, and expect.”.

Ors said he expects the Senate would make changes to the House-passed bill, but he doesn’t know if those changes would come in the form of an amendment or an entirely new bill.

No proposed Senate amendment to the House bill, or alternative Senate bill, has yet to emerge.

He expressed concern over the timeline for reauthorization, especially if the Senate doesn’t take up the House bill as is.

A fresh Senate bill or amendment would require votes in both the House and Senate, with floor time dwindling as both chambers work through must-pass legislation before the end of the year.

Recent findings suggest that congress could potentially pass a short-term reauthorization of FirstNet. Ors expressed worry that option could jeopardize the public-private relationship with contractor AT&T.

Pasco said he would prefer a short reauthorization over the House-passed bill, but said he hopes a full reauthorization could still pass this Congress.

The House bill has strong bipartisan support and the Senate’s negotiations are also bipartisan. Both Ors and Pasco expressed confidence that if time runs out this year for a reauthorization bill, a latest version of the legislation would still have strong prospects under a Democratic Congress.

Additional context regarding the role of FirstNet during the Maui fires was added to this report.

#123868. Blood proteins may flag prostate cancer risk more than a decade before diagnosis

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1305 w)

General ⚠️ Warning 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Blood proteins may flag prostate cancer risk more than a decade before diagnosis

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1305 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Oxford found men's blood differed 15 years before a prostate cancer blood test or diagnosis, with an immune protein among the clearest signs.
  • The blood test men know for prostate cancer measures one protein, PSA, which is made by the prostate itself.
  • The men diagnosed with prostate cancer more than 15 years later already differed in a dozen of them.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Oxford found men's blood differed 15 years before a prostate cancer blood test or diagnosis, with an immune protein among the clearest signs.

The blood test men know for prostate cancer measures one protein, PSA, which is made by the prostate itself. In blood drawn from about 2,500 European men in the 1990s, researchers at Oxford measured more than 6,000 proteins instead.

The men diagnosed with prostate cancer more than 15 years later already differed in a dozen of them.

Sources indicate that one of the clearest differences was an immune protein those men had less of, not more. None of the proteins is ready to become a test, the team remarked. Most of the differences were modest, and not all of them held up in other groups of men.

Zhe Huang, a postdoctoral epidemiologist at Oxford Population Health, part of the University of Oxford, led the work with senior authors Karl Smith-Byrne and Ruth Travis.

Industry observers note that “Prostate cancer is not one disease. Many prostate cancers grow slowly and may never cause harm, while others are aggressive and can be life-threatening,” Huang stated.

The samples came from EPIC, a European health study that recruited more than half a million people in the 1990s and stored their blood.

According to recent reports, huang’s team picked 982 men from Italy, the Netherlands, Spain and the United Kingdom who later developed prostate cancer. They compared them with a random sample of 1,573 men from the same study, followed for a median of about 16 years.

In a recent development, men who developed the disease were a median of about six years older when they gave their blood. So the analysis adjusted for age, along with body mass index, smoking, drinking and education.

The idea was to compare the blood itself, not the men’s ages.

Recent findings suggest that A lab platform called SomaScan measured more than 6,400 proteins in each sample. The team asked which proteins differed years ahead of any diagnosis, and separately which differed ahead of an aggressive cancer.

Aggressive meant high grade, spread beyond the prostate, a very high PSA at diagnosis, or death from the disease, and 290 men fit that definition.

The researchers linked twelve proteins to prostate cancer diagnosed more than 15 years after the blood draw. The clearest was GZMK, a protein made by the immune cells that recognize and destroy abnormal cells.

Men with more GZMK in their blood were less likely to be diagnosed, and the longer the gap to diagnosis, the stronger that link became.

Industry observers note that the authors offered two readings. More GZMK may mean the immune system is doing a better job of clearing early abnormal cells.

Or the men who later developed cancer may have had fewer of those cells in the blood because the cells had moved into the prostate.

In an interview with Earth.com, Huang and Smith-Byrne said researchers generally consider prostate cancer an immunologically “cold” tumor, one that tends to draw a weak immune response.

“This raises interesting questions about the role of the immune system in the very early stages of cancer development,” they added.

Two proteins tied to inflammation, IL-17B and OSCAR, ran the other way. Higher levels went with higher long-term risk.

In a recent development, seven proteins were linked to aggressive prostate cancer. Researchers linked one of them, ANKRD1, to every serious form of the disease examined. These included cancers that had spread and cancers that proved fatal, the authors wrote.

Another, AMIGO2, linked to aggressive disease, and most strongly to cancers that had grown beyond the prostate.

This is an adhesion molecule, part of how cells attach to their surroundings, and lab studies have tied it to the process by which tumor cells break away and travel.

FLT4, a receptor involved in growing fresh blood and lymph vessels, was linked to nearly every outcome the team measured.

The strongest single protein was KLK3, which is PSA under its gene name. Higher PSA levels years earlier increased a man’s likelihood of receiving a diagnosis later.

That isn’t surprising, the authors wrote, because a high PSA reading is what sends a man for a biopsy in the first place.

The team also looked at 71 genes already known to drive prostate cancer when they mutate, and asked whether the proteins those genes produce showed up differently in blood. Five did.

Proteins made by three of those genes, ERBB3, KRAS and NRAS, were linked to aggressive cancers diagnosed about a decade later.

The driver-gene result was the one that surprised the two researchers most.

“These genes are well established in prostate cancer biology, so it was quite surprising to find that their circulating protein products were associated with aggressive prostate cancer,” Huang and Smith-Byrne said.

That doesn’t mean the cancer was already there when the blood was drawn, the authors wrote. Nor is a protein level in blood proof that the gene itself has gone wrong.

Their reading is that the proteins mark early disturbances in the biological pathways to which those genes belong.

According to recent reports, the team checked its findings against a U.S. study of 4,284 men, 590 of whom developed prostate cancer. Only about half of the proteins had been measured there.

Two of them, KLK3 and ACP3, another prostate protein, were clearly linked to the disease there too, and two more indicated the same direction of association.

Industry observers note that several others, including OSCAR, AMIGO2 and FLT4, were associated in opposite directions in Black and White men. The U.S. study had too few Black participants to settle which direction is real, the authors wrote.

In the U.K. Biobank, 18 of the proteins had been measured with a different technology, and the two platforms agreed poorly.

Recent findings suggest that none of those proteins was linked to prostate cancer there. Genetic analyses supported a handful, including AMIGO2, KLK3 and OSCAR.

Recent findings suggest that the aggressive-cancer results also come from fewer men. Tumor grade was unknown for 31 percent of the cases and stage for 46 percent, and only 102 men died of the disease.

Some of the associations may be chance, the authors wrote, and the study had no information on family history.

Whether any of these blood proteins can predict a man’s prostate cancer risk better than his age and PSA already do hasn’t been tested.

Industry observers note that the findings still have to be confirmed in larger and more diverse groups of men, Huang and Smith-Byrne stated. Their study also mainly looked for proteins that may help a prostate cancer develop, not proteins that could spot a cancer already there.

“Developing a blood test for early detection would require further dedicated prediction studies,” they told Earth.com.

Huang said measuring thousands of proteins in blood collected years early lets researchers begin to ask how men who later develop aggressive prostate cancer differ from men who don’t.

The next step runs through a Cancer Research U.K. program on prostate cancer causes and prevention, which the team said will test whether the findings can improve prediction or prevention.

Some of the proteins may even play a causal role in how the cancer develops, the two researchers stated.

“If confirmed by future experimental and clinical studies, this could open up exciting opportunities for earlier prevention, potentially even through approaches such as cancer vaccines,” they said.

In a recent development, for now, the GZMK result is a clue rather than a tool. Men who were never diagnosed had more of an immune protein in their blood 15 years earlier. Whether measuring it would help any patient is the question still open.

The full study was published in the journal European Urology.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that this is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

It has been revealed that yian Yin seeks to understand the dynamics of science itself. The computational social scientist is particularly interested in how innovations happen and how they may be accelerated.

“I want to understand what the secret sources or recipes of success are,” states Yin, of Cornell University.

He applied machine learning techniques to accepted and rejected research proposals to understand how scientists learn from failures. What he found was that scientists fail, and they fail often. Some switched gears after some rejections, but others who continued their research and incorporated feedback found success at a faster rate. Those who changed ideas or scrapped original proposals did not leverage a lot from their experience.

“A group that’s not only failing better and better,” Yin indicates, “is also failing faster and increasingly faster towards their eventual success.”.

According to recent reports, more recently, Yin has been investigating how generative AI is changing scientific publishing. Journals are receiving more AI-assisted submissions than ever before, which is leading the peer-review process to falter. More seemingly well-written papers that lack substance are getting through, he found. Coming up with large-scale solutions requires looking at the glitch in a measurable way, Yin notes.

“Considering both the technological and social side of scientific ecosystems would be something that’s really beneficial for the ongoing public debate and discussion about how we accelerate science in the age of artificial intelligence,” Yin says.

#123866. Industry News: Scientists can now uncover a person’s age, sex, diet, and DNA all from just one single tooth

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1371 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: Scientists can now uncover a person’s age, sex, diet, and DNA all from just one single tooth

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1371 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Forensic scientists sliced a single tooth from each of 15 unidentified bodies and read birth year, age, sex, DNA, diet, and drug use from it.
  • Sources indicate that by the time a body is discovered months or years after death, the face, fingerprints, and clothing are usually long gone.
  • In a recent development, A team in Japan took a single tooth from each of 15 such bodies.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Forensic scientists sliced a single tooth from each of 15 unidentified bodies and read birth year, age, sex, DNA, diet, and drug use from it.

Sources indicate that by the time a body is discovered months or years after death, the face, fingerprints, and clothing are usually long gone. The remaining bones can give investigators a rough idea of sex and age, but that age estimate can be wrong by up to 30 years. Turns out, a single tooth holds far more answers.

In a recent development, A team in Japan took a single tooth from each of 15 such bodies. From that tooth alone, they worked out each person’s birth year, age at death, sex, and DNA profile.

The same tooth also showed what kind of diet the person grew up on and which drugs they had been taking.

Hisako Saitoh, an associate professor of forensic dentistry at the Institute of Science Tokyo, led the work with her doctoral student, Sayaka Yamada.

Fuyuki Tokanai of the Center for Accelerator Mass Spectrometry at Yamagata University was also on the team. Colleagues at the University of Tokyo and Chiba University took part as well.

All 15 people were unidentified when they reached the autopsy table. Five were skeletal remains, ten were badly decomposed. Fourteen of them were later identified.

“Different tissues within a tooth preserve different forensic information. By combining multiple analytical methods, we sought to obtain as many clues as possible from a single tooth,” Saitoh mentioned.

Bone is full of tiny channels for blood vessels and marrow. This means that soil, moisture, and microbes can get into it after death. Enamel is the hardest material in the human body, and it seals the crown of a tooth.

A thin layer called cementum wraps around the root, and this keeps outside substances away from the soft pulp inside.

A tooth also stops changing once it has formed. Bone rebuilds itself throughout life, but enamel laid down in early childhood stays chemically the same until death.

That makes a tooth a sealed record of the years when it grew. This explains why researchers have used teeth to track where a mammoth or an elephant once lived.

Earlier forensic teams had combined several of these tests, but they used several teeth per person, or a tooth plus a toenail, and the bodies hadn’t been dead for long.

Saitoh’s team wanted to know how much information one tooth could provide after a body had been lying outdoors for months or years.

The team chose the lower first premolar, the tooth just behind the canine. Its crown finishes forming at about age five, so its enamel records the first years of life. It has a single root, it’s easy to pull, and the lips cover the gap it leaves.

Each tooth was washed, dried overnight, and cut lengthwise into slices about 1/25 of an inch (1 millimeter) thick, which is thinner than a dime.

It has been revealed that enamel from one slice went to a radiocarbon lab, and a root slice rich in cementum went to DNA testing. Dentin from the other side went to an age test, and the central slice holding the pulp went to drug screening.

It has been revealed that the age test relies on a slow chemical change. Amino acids in living tissue come in a left-handed form, and over a lifetime a small share flips to the right-handed mirror image.

The team measured that share in the dentin and read the person’s age off a curve built from six other premolars of known age.

The birth year came from radiocarbon, but not the kind used on fossils. Nuclear weapons tests in the 1950s and early 1960s sharply raised the amount of radioactive carbon in the air. The level peaked in 1963 and has been falling ever since.

Enamel forming in a child’s mouth took up whatever level was in the air at the time, so its carbon highlights when it formed. Scientists have used the same spike to age a whale from its teeth.

Sources indicate that the catch is that the curve rises and then falls, so one reading usually matches two possible years. For one man, the enamel gave a birth year of either 1955 or 1979.

In a recent development, adding the age-at-death estimate settled it. A birth in 1979 plus his estimated 58 years would put his death in 2036, so he was born in 1955. His real birth year was 1957.

Recent findings suggest that across the 15 people, the radiocarbon ranges included the true birth year in 14 cases. The age-at-death estimates on their own were off by about eight years on average.

Once the two tests were combined, the birth-year estimates landed within about five years of the truth, on average.

DNA from the cementum slice gave the person’s sex in all 15 cases. In 12 of them it also produced a profile with enough genetic markers to match against a relative or a database.

The same kind of DNA work has recently corrected the story of a Roman-era skeleton in England and been read from Neanderthal teeth.

In a recent development, the pulp slice went through a drug screen covering 251 substances, and every one of the 15 teeth contained something, even if only caffeine. In nine cases the drugs in the tooth matched at least some of what the original autopsy had found in blood or muscle.

In five cases they matched prescriptions the person was known to have been taking, including antidepressants and antipsychotics.

Recent findings suggest that the tooth didn’t catch everything, however. Drugs that appeared to have been taken shortly before death indicated up in stomach contents and muscle at autopsy but not in the tooth.

Saitoh’s team suggested that drugs move into a tooth slowly, so a tooth reflects long-term use rather than a last dose.

According to recent reports, the fifteenth body belonged to a man who has never been definitively identified. His tooth put his birth year at either 1956 or 1976, and his dentin put his age at about 38.

The 1956 option would mean he died in 1995, long before his body was found in 2013, so the team’s answer is a man born in 1976.

It has been revealed that investigators right now believe he was born around 1972 and was about 41 when he died. The two readings disagree by four years, which is inside the method’s average error of about five years.

The tooth gives investigators a second, independent estimate of who he might be.

Stable carbon in the enamel added a rough picture of childhood diet. All 15 readings fit a diet built on rice and wheat rather than corn, which is consistent with a traditional Japanese diet.

The authors wrote that carbon alone can’t say where someone grew up.

Recent findings suggest that the errors here were larger than in earlier studies that ran each test on its own. The birth-year estimates were least accurate for people born before the fallout spike began to climb and for those born in more recent years, when the curve had flattened.

It has been revealed that the age test usually works best on dentin from the center of the tooth. Here the center was needed for the drug screen. Instead, the team used dentin from the outer part, and that may have cost some accuracy.

One tooth also produced radiocarbon dates between the 600s and 800s AD, centuries before the woman could have been born.

That sample had the highest carbon content of the set, and the authors suspect carbon from outside the body had got into the enamel.

The team’s next step is more cases, and a closer look at exactly where in a tooth each slice should come from.

“Moving forward, we aim to further improve the accuracy and reproducibility of each biochemical analytical method demonstrated in this study and establish standardized methods that can be widely applied in routine forensic medical and dental practice,” Saitoh said.

The full study was published in the journal Scientific Reports.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • Here’s what you’ll learn when you read this story:.
  • I clearly remember the very last time I used one of my reliable old pyrex baking dishes, and it makes me blush.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Here’s what you’ll learn when you read this story:.

I clearly remember the very last time I used one of my reliable old pyrex baking dishes, and it makes me blush. I was making a chicken recipe but had forgotten to add enough liquid to the pan. In the interest of saving time, I took the hot pan out of the oven, opened a carton of chicken stock from the fridge, and tipped a little in. That’s when my pyrex baking dish shattered into three or four large glass shards, mingled with the now ruined chicken. It broke apart the moment the cold stock touched the hot glass.

It has been revealed that though I was shocked, I realized what my mistake was—the glass couldn’t bear the sudden temperature change. But it made me wonder: wasn’t pyrex designed specifically to hold its structural integrity under just these kinds of temperature fluctuations? When I started searching, I found that people have been complaining about their pyrex cookware exploding for years. Perhaps they just weren’t reading the instructions. Then, I stumbled across a different reason for my destroyed dinner: there’s pyrex, and then there’s PYREX.

Recent findings suggest that the first experiment to use PYREX for cooking took place more than a century ago, in the kitchen of Corning Glass Works physicist Jesse T. Littleton, whose wife used a sawn-off glass battery jar to bake in the oven. It was made of borosilicate and that was the key. Used today in cookware and lab equipment such as beakers, Corning’s “Nonex” glass was invented for hot, burning-oil railway lanterns that needed to stay intact when exposed to cold weather. Calling it fire-glass, the manufacturer later named it PYREX®, a play on the word “pyro,” meaning “fire” in Greek, and “ex,” from the label that identified its earlier product.

Since then, PYREX has withstood the intense temperatures and harsh chemical onslaughts of laboratory work. It works well for temperatures of up to 425 degrees Fahrenheit in household kitchens.

It has been revealed that the secret to the original PYREX’s heat resilience is its borosilicate composition, a glass made of silica and boron trioxide. Glass expands when it’s hot and contracts while cooling. Heat causes its atoms to vibrate and move apart, weakening the glass. However, boron atoms don’t vibrate or separate as much as other elements, making the overall glass more stable.

It has been revealed that around the 1950s, Corning also began making PYREX bakeware out of tempered soda lime glass, according to Smithsonian magazine. In 1998, Corning sold its consumer product operations to Borden, later renamed World Kitchen, then Corelle Brands. Corelle continued to produce the tempered soda lime bakeware in America—this is called “pyrex,” all lowercase. These days, Corning only makes PYREX borosilicate labware products, such as beakers, for scientific use. In Europe, the brand International Cookware still makes borosilicate cookware.

Industry observers note that ✅ To have a more accurate idea of what you're buying, here’s a good rule of thumb: “Pyrex” is a brand name with clear distinctions depending on how it’s written. Only cookware marked “PYREX”—all uppercase—is likely made of borosilicate glass. However, most of this is made in Europe; lowercase pyrex brand cookware made in the U.S. has been tempered soda lime for decades. It’s still possible to locate some Pyrex brand borosilicate cookware in the U.S., but it’s harder to find. If you see the label “pyrex,” it definitely means the glass is made of tempered soda lime.

In a recent development, despite its deep roots in American kitchens, home cooks have been complaining about pyrex shattering in the oven or during rapid temperature changes since the early 2000s. In 2010, the nonprofit organization Consumer Reports released a warning following a yearlong investigation of pyrex shattering incidents. “When we examined 163 incidents in detail, we discovered at least 42 reports of injuries. While hundreds of millions of dishes are used safely each year, we believe the situation is serious enough that we have asked the Consumer Product Safety Commission to investigate,” according to the report.

During testing, soda lime glass shattered at lower temperatures than “more expensive” borosilicate Pyrex bakeware, the report continued. Consumer Reports found that the iconic glass bakeware produced in America today is of soda lime, while the European-made products investigators tested were borosilicate.

Consumers also complained that the manufacturer’s instructions were confusing. Consumer Reports found that the small print on the back of products containing the necessary precautions is “easy to miss.”.

Borosilicate glass can withstand up to three times as much thermal shock as soda lime silicate. “When glass bakeware does shatter, consumers report, it can break into sharp shards that go flying, raising the risks of injuries. This contrasts with claims from one of the manufacturers that its glass bakeware breaks into ‘relatively small pieces generally lacking sharp edges,’” according to the report.

Sources indicate that soda lime glass is made of about 60 to 75 percent silica, 12 to 18 percent soda, and 5 to 12 percent lime. Heat-treated and then rapidly cooled on its exterior, the outside of tempered soda lime glass solidifies more swiftly than the center. While cooling, the inside pulls at the stiffer exterior layer, creating tension that makes the whole piece more durable. If it does break, tempered glass forms rounded, cube-shaped chunks, instead of the sharp shards of untempered soda lime glass—think about the last time you dropped a drinking glass.

Industry observers note that untempered soda lime glass is used for items that aren’t supposed to be heated, such as drinking glasses and windows. It isn’t safe for either the oven or the microwave oven.

So look for a European provenance, or simply “borosilicate” in the description before you buy your next glass baking dish. I know I will, because I’m pretty sure I’ve only ever owned the soda lime version.

#123864. Ice Age humans were far less isolated than scientists assumed, according to a 30,000-year-old woman’s DNA

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1397 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Ice Age humans were far less isolated than scientists assumed, according to a 30,000-year-old woman’s DNA

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1397 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ice Age Europeans mixed across the continent earlier than genetics had shown, according to a 30,000-year-old genome and DNA from cave dirt.
  • Most people imagine Ice Age Europe as a patchwork of tiny hunting bands living out their lives in isolated valleys, far from any other group.
  • Archaeologists have doubted that version of history for a long time.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ice Age Europeans mixed across the continent earlier than genetics had shown, according to a 30,000-year-old genome and DNA from cave dirt.

Most people imagine Ice Age Europe as a patchwork of tiny hunting bands living out their lives in isolated valleys, far from any other group.

Archaeologists have doubted that version of history for a long time. This is mainly due to the fact that the same styles of tools and carvings show up across the entire continent. Even so, DNA from Ice Age samples has mostly supported the isolated view.

A woman who died around 30,000 years ago in what is now southwestern France has changed that.

Most of her ancestry came from the western European people of her time. However, part of it also came from populations related to central and eastern Europe. The mixing happened roughly 32,500 to 31,500 years ago.

The analysis of her DNA now gives the oldest set of genome-wide data from a modern human in southwestern Europe.

In a recent development, pere Gelabert and Ron Pinhasi of the University of Vienna‘s Department of Evolutionary Anthropology led the work. Their co-authors include researchers at Harvard Medical School, the University of Cantabria and the University of New Mexico.

The study rests on DNA from three new Ice Age individuals and one sample of cave sediment. Thus, the picture it draws is built from very few people.

It has been revealed that the bone fragment of the woman was recovered from Isturitz Cave in the Basque Country, western Pyrenees. Excavators dug it up in the 1950s, and it stayed in a Paris institute for over 60 years. Then, in 2013, Pinhasi took a sample from it for DNA analysis.

Recent findings suggest that the team recovered more than 454,000 of the genetic markers it was looking for. This represents one of the richest Gravettian datasets yet.

Gravettian is the name for the culture that spread across Europe during the onset of the last Ice Age, between about 34,000 and 25,000 years ago. This culture is known for its shared tool styles, burial practices and portable art.

Until now, DNA data from this Ice Age period in Europe sorted into two stable groups, a western one and a central-eastern one, with little sign of contact between them.

It has been revealed that the Isturitz woman belongs mostly to the western group. But several tests also found a share of her ancestry related to the ancestors of people buried at Dolní Věstonice in what is now the Czech Republic.

In an interview with Earth.com, Gelabert said the find overturned a long-held assumption.

“Until this latest genomic data, we assumed that the people in Southwestern Europe were quite the same for more than 20,000 years,” he said.

The latest data, he stated, point to population movements that were probably continental in scale, and that the team doesn’t yet clearly understand.

Isturitz is one of the richest Ice Age sites in southern Europe, with an unusual number of carved objects and signs of repeated, intensive occupation.

Sources indicate that archaeologists have long argued that it was a gathering place where different groups met to hunt, trade, socialize and find partners. The cave lies at the natural passage between the rest of Europe and the Iberian Peninsula.

The woman isn’t alone. When the team reanalyzed a previously published genome from Ormesson, near Paris, dated to about 31,800 to 30,000 years ago, it found a similar eastern signal.

In addition, Belgian individuals from Goyet Cave, about 28,000 to 26,000 years old, were already known to carry mixed ancestry.

Industry observers note that two explanations are possible, the authors wrote. People from the east may have moved west during the Gravettian itself. Or the eastern-looking ancestry may be an older component, already in western Europe before 35,000 years ago.

The team favors the first. The DNA signal is absent from earlier Ice Age genomes in the same region, and it vanishes from southwestern Europe after 30,000 years ago.

At El Mirón Cave in Cantabria, northern Spain, the team took two pinches of sediment, 0.002 ounces (50 milligrams) each.

They came from a layer dated to about 22,100 to 21,700 years ago, the coldest stretch of the last Ice Age, when human remains are extremely rare. No bone or tooth was needed, only the dirt that people had walked on.

The researchers built nine DNA libraries from those two extracts and sequenced them 101 times. Out of roughly a billion DNA fragments, more than 294,000 were human.

After the team kept only fragments showing the chemical damage of real ancient DNA, 14,737 genetic markers remained, enough to read the ancestry of the people who used the cave.

The sediment’s ancestry matched the western group, the Isturitz woman’s lineage, so that ancestry persisted in the region through the coldest millennia.

It has been revealed that “Sedimentary DNA allows us to recover genetic information from periods where human remains are missing,” Pinhasi said. “This gives us a way to connect archaeological layers with the genetic ancestry of the people who occupied a site.”.

Gelabert told Earth.com the team had recovered DNA from this cave’s sediment before. “What surprised us this time is that the quality is unmatched,” he mentioned.

Industry observers note that he described the sample as one of the richest sources of human DNA ever reported. For the first time in the region’s Upper Paleolithic, he said, it let the team tie a culture to a group of people.

The third upcoming genome came from Ostuni Cave in southern Italy and belongs to a male fetus about 27,800 to 27,400 years old.

It has been revealed that the team identified him as a first-degree relative of a woman from the same cave whose genome was already published. He was most likely her son.

It has been revealed that comparing the two showed that his father came from the same population as his mother, as far as the data can tell. Yet the parents were not close relatives.

The boy’s genome carried no long stretches of identical DNA from both parents, and the population he came from was genetically larger than any other Gravettian group measured so far.

Gelabert remarked this is the first mother-and-fetus pair of genomes from the European Paleolithic, and that comparing them is what indicated how genetically diverse her population was.

All three individuals, and the people in the El Mirón sediment, are predicted to have had dark skin, dark hair and brown eyes. That was the usual pattern for Europeans of that era.

The whole Gravettian, Solutrean and Epigravettian record, three Ice Age cultures, rests on genome-wide data from fewer than 50 people. This study adds an extra three.

The third is a tooth from Chufín Cave in Cantabria, dated to about 26,000 years ago. It was so degraded that it yielded fewer than 20,000 markers, enough to place it in the western group and little more.

According to recent reports, sediment has its own limits. The DNA in it comes from several people mixed together, and the team’s reading suggests more of them were male than female. The date for the east-west mixing also assumes it happened in a single pulse.

The study does not settle where the eastern ancestry came from. The authors wrote that no particular central European group stands out as the source, and that no genome from the earlier Aurignacian culture exists for southwestern Europe to compare against.

The team did find one thing the data argue against. Earlier work on tooth shapes had suggested a population turnover in western Europe around 28,000 years ago.

The upcoming genomes, the sediment and the reanalyzed published data instead show the same western ancestry in place from 30,000 to 20,000 years ago.

Asked by Earth.com what comes next, Gelabert returned to the sediment.

Industry observers note that “Next step is clearly to find out when the population movements that we see in Isturitz really happened. Sediment will be key for this goal,” he noted.

The authors named a target: the Aurignacian layers of Isturitz itself, deposits older than the woman, which could show whether the eastern signal was already there before she was born.

The full study was published in the journal Science Advances.

A Woman Left Her Belongings in Pompeii Nearly 2,000 Years Ago. Archaeologists Just Found Them.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • It has been revealed that the house in question likely belonged to Cornelius Maxium, based on inscriptions no longer visible but seen during a 1912 excavation.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a centrally located home in ancient Pompeii’s Via dell’Abbondanza (translated as Street of Abundance), one woman curated a cozy—and intimate—dressing room, obscured by a façade. The identity of the woman is itself now obscured and lost to time, but the eruption of Mount Vesuvius in 79 C.E. froze her personal habits and routines in ash. 2,000 years later, archaeologists found it exactly as it was.

It has been revealed that the house in question likely belonged to Cornelius Maxium, based on inscriptions no longer visible but seen during a 1912 excavation. Archaeologists recently ventured behind the home’s façade, and in doing so, opened a wardrobe last opened in 79 C.E.

According to recent reports, archaeologists spelled out the find in an online excavation journal from Pompeii Sites, highlighting how the investigation revealed the woman’s personal beauty routine and daily habits. The wardrobe contained cosmetic tools of tweezers and a mixing palette, a glass perfume vial, an incense burner, and a bronze oil lamp. The excavation also revealed vessels and pots of bronze, glass, and ceramic, as well as a small wooden box contained lead weights, which were likely used in trading.

It has been revealed that “Pompeii is not just a place of great works of art; it is also a place where the most ordinary objects reveal the human dimension of the past,” Gabriel Zuchtriegel, director of the Pompeii Archaeological Park, stated in a translated statement. “The value of this discovery lies in the ability to piece together various traces of a life—personal habits, work, and memories. While we cannot reconstruct the identity of the house’s inhabitant with certainty, these fragments bring us closer to their daily existence.”.

Recent findings suggest that the woman whose wardrobe this was, for example, may have had a great affection for pinecones. In addition to the discovery of a small jug decorated with a pinecone motif, there was also a necklace with at least 24 miniature charms made from faience, bone, glass paste, and rock crystals. Some of those charms also depicted pinecones.

Sources indicate that tucked inside a cloth pouch inside the wardrobe, archaeologists may have found the most personal item of all: a necklace with amulets known as “crepundia,” which literally translates to rattles. Typically worn by children for ritual protection—the amulets were thought to contain spells that offered protection—the items also audibly rattled so adults could better track their children’s movements.

Recent findings suggest that roman-era experts said adults often kept childhood crepundia as a keepsake. “The Roman world was characterized by a high degree of geographical mobility at every social level, from slaves to wealthy merchants,” according to the statement. “As a result, many people found themselves living far from the parents, relatives, and the places where they had grown up.”.

Amidst the personal items at Via dell’Abbondanza, archeologists may have located the woman’s proto-piggy bank, as excavations revealed a woven container holding 38 bronze coins.

That such deeply personal items, to say nothing of the hoard of bronze coins, were there within the wardrobe to be found centuries later suggests that the owner, whoever she may have been, fled the eruption and subsequent devastation with no time to extract them, and never returned to retrieve them. That, of course, is assuming they survived to even attempt it.

In a recent development, it’s possible the owners were not home at the time of the eruption, as the room housing the wardrobe appeared to be under some level of renovation when the disaster occurred. Even in its mid-reno state, however, the room featured expensive Italian paintings, highlighting the potential wealth of the occupants that match the prime real estate along one of the ancient city’s main thoroughfares. The excavation also uncovered the remains of some of the home’s smaller residents when Vesuvius rained down its devastation. There was a pair of young wood mice skeletons inside an amphora on the home’s mezzanine level, showing that even the finest urban homes in Pompeii clashed with rodents. Evidently, there was no crepundia warding them off.

#123862. Air pollution may weaken one of the brain’s natural defenses against dementia

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1079 w)
📖 Baca
General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Air pollution may weaken one of the brain’s natural defenses against dementia

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1079 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A mouse study suggests that fine particles in polluted air can weaken the brain’s protective barrier, offering a clue to the link between air pollution and dementia.
  • Recent findings suggest that air pollution has been linked to dementia for years.
  • It has been revealed that an experiment in Ohio has provided some clues.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A mouse study suggests that fine particles in polluted air can weaken the brain’s protective barrier, offering a clue to the link between air pollution and dementia.

Recent findings suggest that air pollution has been linked to dementia for years. It is difficult, however, to work out what happens inside the brain between the time a person breathes in polluted air and the onset of memory problems.

It has been revealed that an experiment in Ohio has provided some clues. After months of breathing polluted air, laboratory mice kept their weight, groomed themselves and went about their usual activities without obvious signs of distress.

Put those same mice in a maze they had already learned to navigate, though, and something was wrong.

Changes had taken place inside their brains, even in animals that had no genetic predisposition to Alzheimer’s-like disease.

Before working with mice, the team examined health records from 475,325 adults enrolled in the UK Biobank between 2006 and 2010.

The median age at enrollment was 58. Over a median follow-up period of nearly 14 years, 12,758 participants developed Alzheimer’s disease or a related dementia or died of an Alzheimer’s-related cause.

The researchers wanted to know how much of the risk was associated with where people lived and how much was associated with their genes.

Higher levels of fine particle pollution were linked to dementia, even after accounting for factors such as smoking and diabetes.

People with greater inherited susceptibility also faced higher risk, although the combined association was smaller than expected if the two individual effects multiplied.

For the animal experiments, the team used air collected outdoors in Cleveland, Ohio.

The particles of interest were PM2.5, a group of airborne particles measuring about one ten-thousandth of an inch (2.5 micrometers) or less.

The samples contained a mixture of substances associated with dust and combustion, including iron, nickel and copper.

In a recent development, the team concentrated the particles until their levels reached roughly 10 times those measured outdoors in Cleveland. The resulting concentration was comparable to the average reported for Newly introduced Delhi in 2023.

At just four weeks old, mice began breathing either this polluted air or filtered air for eight hours a day, five days a week. Among them were animals carrying five genetic mutations associated with inherited Alzheimer’s disease.

Sixteen weeks into the experiment, the team began testing the animals’ memory.

One test involved a circular platform with an escape hole. Over three days, the mice had repeated opportunities to learn where the hole was, followed by a two-day break before their final test.

Ordinary mice breathing polluted air had about as much difficulty finding the hole as Alzheimer’s-prone mice breathing filtered air. The genetically vulnerable mice exposed to pollution struggled the most.

Other tests revealed problems recognizing unfamiliar objects, weaker muscles in the front and back legs, and behavior consistent with increased anxiety.

Blood vessels in the brain have a protective barrier that limits what can pass from the blood into surrounding brain tissue. Without a properly functioning barrier, potentially harmful substances have easier access to that tissue.

To check for leaks, the team used three chemical markers, including a blue dye.

Much more of these substances escaped from blood vessels in pollution-exposed mice than in ordinary mice breathing filtered air.

Some of the leakage measurements, however, came from groups of as few as two animals.

The brains of exposed mice also contained higher levels of several chemicals involved in inflammation.

Whether the inflammation damaged blood vessels or whether other processes contributed to both problems remains unclear.

In a recent development, within the hippocampus, a region involved in forming memories, lies a smaller area called the dentate gyrus. Newly introduced brain cells continue to form there after birth in mice.

Interestingly, pollution did not significantly affect how many new cells ordinary mice produced. The problem was keeping those cells alive, as fewer survived over a period of 30 days.

In mice prone to Alzheimer’s disease, both the production and survival of latest cells suffered.

Pollution also disturbed the balance between two forms of a molecule called NAD, which cells depend on for energy production and processes involved in repairing damage.

Much of the investigation centered on microglia, the immune cells that live inside the brain. Sanjay Rajagopalan, a professor of medicine at Case Western Reserve University, co-led the work.

“By recreating in mice what happens when people breath polluted air, we found that pollution causes major changes in which genes are active in the brain’s immune cells,” mentioned Sanjay Rajagopalan.

It has been revealed that when the researchers compared polluted-air and filtered-air groups, they identified changes in the activity of 766 genes in ordinary mice. They also found that genetic background influenced how 2,876 genes responded to pollution.

“These cells normally keep the brain healthy by clearing away debris and fighting infection. Seeing how pollution disrupts them helps explain how a stress that affects much of the world’s population harms the brain, and it points us toward a way to treat it,” Rajagopalan stated.

In a recent development, alzheimer’s disease is associated with the accumulation of a protein called amyloid in the brain. As the protein collects, it forms deposits known as plaques.

Despite examining brain tissue with two different staining methods, the team could not find these plaques in ordinary mice that had breathed polluted air. Their memory problems had developed without detectable amyloid buildup.

Andrew Pieper, a professor of translational psychiatry at Case Western Reserve University, was also a senior author.

“We’ve identified a key way that air pollution harms the healthy brain and speeds up Alzheimer’s disease,” noted Andrew Pieper.

Recent findings suggest that how much pollution each person actually breathed remains unknown. The team estimated exposure using home addresses.

It has been revealed that only white participants and male mice were studied. Gene analysis involved just three mice per group.

In a recent development, “This helps us understand how factors in our environment can accelerate and intensify brain diseases of aging. It also opens the door to studying other environmental stresses on the brain, and to finding ways to keep the brain resilient even when we can’t avoid those stressors,” Pieper mentioned.

Air pollution’s role in human dementia needs further investigation. But unlike inherited risk, pollution can be reduced.

The full study was published in the Journal of Neuroinflammation.
