Rainbow trout faced a familiar virus, but tiny plastic fibers changed their chances of survival

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (993 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a lab study, young rainbow trout exposed to nylon microfibers were less likely to survive a common fish virus.
  • Microplastics come in many shapes, and a new study on rainbow trout suggests the shape matters.
  • In an eight-week experiment, young trout exposed to both nylon microplastic fibers and a common fish virus had roughly double the odds of dying compared with trout exposed to the virus alone.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a lab study, young rainbow trout exposed to nylon microfibers were less likely to survive a common fish virus.

Microplastics come in many shapes, and a new study on rainbow trout suggests the shape matters.

In an eight-week experiment, young trout exposed to both nylon microplastic fibers and a common fish virus had roughly double the odds of dying compared with trout exposed to the virus alone.

Trout that lived with round nylon particles of similar width fared no worse than fish with no plastic at all.

Sources indicate that the fibers didn’t kill fish on their own. Without the virus, plastic of either shape made no difference to survival.

The study came from the Virginia Institute of Marine Science at William & Mary, where Meredith Evans Seeley, Robert Hale and Andrew Wargo work. Anna Mehlhorn, an undergraduate at the time, is now at Cornell.

“Not all plastics are created equal, and so that creates an opportunity to identify the worst forms of pollution and come up with solutions,” Wargo remarked.

It has been revealed that three years ago, the same group reported that microplastics made a trout virus deadlier. Nylon microfibers stood out: in that earlier work, fish exposed to them faced a hazard of death 6.4 times that of fish given the virus alone.

“We saw the effect with the nylon fibers and had to ask, ‘Is it the fact it’s a fiber or is it the fact that it was nylon?'” Hale said.

To answer that, the team kept the material the same and changed the shape. The fibers were about 0.02 inches (500 micrometers) long and 10 micrometers wide, the kind that shed from synthetic fabric.

The powder was made of rounded nylon grains averaging 15 to 20 micrometers across, about as wide as the fibers but nowhere near as long.

In a recent development, the team raised 800 juvenile rainbow trout in 40 tanks of 20 fish each. Every other day, the plastic groups got a dose of fibers or powder in their water, and the tank sat still for a day before it was flushed.

Most groups got plastic for the full eight weeks; two fiber groups got it only in the first or last four.

Halfway through, half the tanks were dosed with infectious hematopoietic necrosis virus, a major cause of losses on trout farms.

Fish started dying a few days later, and the dying largely ended within about two weeks.

By the end, 39% of the trout exposed to both the virus and eight weeks of fibers were alive. In tanks that got the virus with no plastic, 56% survived, and in tanks with neither, 86% did.

In the statistical model, eight weeks of fibers raised the odds of death 2.03 times compared with no particles.

None of the other plastic treatments had a significant effect, including the round powder for eight weeks and the fibers given only before or only after the virus.

Sources indicate that the team also sampled tank water every few days to measure how much virus the fish were shedding. Shedding peaked three days after the virus went in and fell to undetectable levels by day 47 in every treatment.

The plastic groups did not differ, though the eight-week fiber tanks highlighted a trend toward the highest peaks.

The authors wrote that measuring shedding from groups of fish in only four tanks per treatment may have limited the study’s power. A few super-shedders could mask the rest.

Sources indicate that so the fibers did not seem to make the virus more abundant. They seemed to make the fish easier to infect.

The researchers suspect the long, stiff fibers damage protective tissue such as the gills, which they described in the university’s account as the fibers’ pokiness.

“It’s likely creating an easier path for that virus to infect that host,” Seeley remarked.

If microplastic fibers open a door for the virus, the damage has to be there before the virus arrives, and it probably has to keep up afterward. That is what the tanks demonstrated.

Fibers given only after infection did about as well as no plastic. Fibers given only before the virus pushed mortality up toward the chronic group’s level, but the difference was not significant.

The authors pointed to tissue damage from plastic in other animals. In seabirds, scarring from swallowed plastic has been given its own name, plasticosis. Inflammation from microplastics is also under study in fish and in human tissue.

“One of the things that was becoming clear to us is that microplastics have really significant impacts, but they’re not always lethal,” Seeley mentioned.

The team used one high concentration of plastic, 10 milligrams per liter, to make the effect easy to see. The authors wrote that future work should test a range of doses to find the levels that matter in real water.

The fibers and the powder were also not chemically identical, since the fibers were a stiffer grade of nylon.

The work was funded by the NOAA Marine Debris Program. The group is now working with a commercial trout farm to find out which microplastics turn up in working tanks and where they come from.

Trout farms use nylon line and other plastic gear that can break down into microplastics, and the particles are also common in the water where wild fish live.

Earlier work has shown that microplastics can carry microbes and change how pathogens behave.

Recent findings suggest that people are also exposed to microplastic fibers through indoor dust. The authors wrote that the results call for research into whether microplastics change the course of infectious disease in wildlife and people.

They also want to know which features of a particle, such as rigidity and length, do the damage.

The full study was published in the journal Environmental Toxicology and Chemistry.

In an increasingly fire-prone western North America, Jennifer Grenz, an ecologist and member of the Lytton First Nation, looks at fire with a holistic eye. She considers her work with landscapes recovering from catastrophic wildfire to be “deliberately unfocused,” spanning soil microbial ecology, restoration ecology, invasion biology and historical biology.

In a recent development, grenz analyzes historical ecological records, like how Indigenous people have shaped and cared for ecosystems over time, to paint a comprehensive picture. “I’m interested in how those histories leave ecological legacies and hints of the stewardship of the past,” claims Grenz, who leads the Indigenous Ecology Lab at the University of British Columbia in Canada. “What changed on the land that made it more vulnerable?”.

Grenz spends time with many kinds of specialists, such as archaeologists, anthropologists and Indigenous elders who provide oral histories.

Moving forward, her lab will examine ecology below ground, including soil, microbial communities and root networks. The goal is to understand the role of underground ecology in critical topics like carbon sequestration, climate change, biodiversity and sustainable management.

“My motivation is in our interior Salish Territories in the southern interior of British Columbia, where my ancestors rest and where my people are,” Grenz says. “The responsibility I feel to them and to our Tmícw, which means our lands, [is] to not take us back to the past, but to show that we have the deep knowledge to help us move forward.”.

  • When a team of researchers from Princeton and the University of Wisconsin-Madison gauged the theoretical destruction of a nuclear strike in low-Earth orbit, or LEO, the results were grim.
  • “Radiation-disabled spacecraft remain in orbit but are assumed to lose maneuverability,” they said in a study recently posted to the preprint server arXiv.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If hypothetical aliens ever search for technosignatures, thousands upon thousands of satellites orbiting Earth should be an obvious sign that intelligent life exists on this planet. The problem is that an alien spacecraft might be better off keeping its distance. As the spiral into dystopia here on Earth continues, there has been growing concern that someone could take out many of those satellites (and the infrastructure they support) with a nuclear weapon. What would happen in the wake of such an attack is a question keeping scientists from sleeping at night.

When a team of researchers from Princeton and the University of Wisconsin-Madison gauged the theoretical destruction of a nuclear strike in low-Earth orbit, or LEO, the results were grim. There have been over 13,000 satellites at altitudes under 1,242 miles (2,000 km) since early 2026. Many of these fly close together in a region of about 193-232 square miles (500-600 km2), and the use of LEO has only been expanding as the U.S. Department of Defense continues deploying hundreds more for detecting missiles and carrying out military communications, but they have only become more of a target for hostile forces. In an unnerving thought experiment, the researchers worked out the aftermath of detonating a one-megaton nuclear weapon 311 miles (500 kilometers) above the South Atlantic—they found it would easily wipe out about 98% of satellites.

“Radiation-disabled spacecraft remain in orbit but are assumed to lose maneuverability,” they said in a study recently posted to the preprint server arXiv. “We follow collisions and breakup fragments in altitude bands, retaining mass and allowing fragments to move above and below their birth altitude after a velocity kick. Both intact objects and debris descend under atmospheric drag.”.

Sources indicate that this is not the first time a “what if” like has been batted around, in theory or otherwise. Nuclear paranoia decades ago led to an actual experiment that revealed the potential horrors of detonating something in LEO. On July 9, 1962, the the Starfish Prime test saw a 1.4-megaton bomb detonated in the Pacific, around 400 km above Johnston Atoll. An artificial radiation belt was created by clouds of electrons released from radioactive debris scattered by nuclear fission. It caused severe damage to satellites that were either in outfit at the time or debuted soon afterward. Radiation continues to be dangerous long after the initial explosion, because spacecraft continue to pass through it as they orbit, experiencing degrading effects that make them more difficult to maneuver. They then end up at increased risk of collision.

It has been revealed that the researchers found that the worst effects from a detonation over the South Atlantic would be from exposure to radiation damage, which would disable 25% of the fleet in not even a day. That would rocket to 78% after three days and 98% after a week. Damaged satellites prone to crashing would collide with each other—or scraps of space junk—and gradually shut down services that rely on them. There would be three collisions within 15 days and double that by 30. Smashing spacecraft would also clog LEO with fragments that would put even more satellites at risk, and at least 19 collisions would occur a year after the detonation. Atmospheric drag would reduce the hazard by removing disabled spacecraft orbiting lower, but those at higher altitudes would remain at the highest risk. Disabled satellites would continue to die off.

Recent findings suggest that starfish Prime was so disastrous that the Partial Nuclear Test Ban Treaty was signed by the U.S. and the Soviet Union a year later. This enforced an outright ban on testing nuclear weapons anywhere but underground, whether it was on the surface, in the atmosphere, or deep in space. Satellites in LEO have multiplied since the 1960s. How long radioactive ions can keep letting electrons loose above the atmosphere is still uncertain, but satellite breakdowns would be staggering. It would take decades to restore the damaged spacecraft and infrastructure.

“Restoring orbital services would require more than replacing the lost spacecraft,” the researchers said. “Fresh satellites would need to survive the remaining radiation and debris. The prospect of rapid infrastructure loss followed by years of disruption reinforces the need to prevent the deployment and use of nuclear weapons in space.”.

#123858. Prohibition helped save diamondback terrapins from the soup pot, and now a tiny parasite hints their subspecies line may be in the wrong place

Prohibition helped save diamondback terrapins from the soup pot, and now a tiny parasite hints their subspecies line may be in the wrong place

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (936 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A fluke that lives in mudsnails and diamondback terrapins shows a genetic break near the Carolinas border, up to about 186 miles south of the turtles' subspecies line.
  • Diamondback terrapins are hard to count.
  • According to recent reports, A tiny flatworm that depends on them is easier to find.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A fluke that lives in mudsnails and diamondback terrapins shows a genetic break near the Carolinas border, up to about 186 miles south of the turtles' subspecies line.

Diamondback terrapins are hard to count. They live in scattered coastal marshes, travel little, and are scarce in many places.

According to recent reports, A tiny flatworm that depends on them is easier to find. It leaves pearly cysts on mudsnails, and even community volunteers can spot them.

Scientists have now read the DNA of that parasite at marshes from Cape Cod to northeast Florida.

Its populations split near the North Carolina and South Carolina border, up to about 186 miles (300 kilometers) south of where the line between two terrapin subspecies is usually drawn.

The parasite is a fluke called Pleurogonius malaclemys. Adult flukes live and mate in the intestines of diamondback terrapins, and their eggs leave the turtle in its droppings.

Eastern mudsnails then eat the eggs. Inside a snail, the fluke multiplies without mating and sends out larvae that settle on snails, mostly on the plate that seals the shell, as small, pearly cysts.

When a terrapin eats a snail carrying cysts, the cycle starts again.

Because the fluke cannot complete its life without terrapins, its cysts on snails are a sign that terrapins live nearby.

Snails only pick up the fluke as adults, after their drifting larval stage, so the parasite’s travel between marshes is likely to depend mostly on the turtles.

Industry observers note that diamondback terrapins are the only turtle in North America that lives only in brackish coastal water. Until the early 20th century they were hunted heavily for turtle soup, and populations crashed.

It has been revealed that prohibition helped them. In 1920 it banned sherry, a key ingredient in most turtle soup recipes, and the hunting pressure largely faded.

Numbers kept falling anyway, because of habitat loss and terrapins getting caught in crab pots. The coastal marshes they depend on are under threat too, and nearly all of the world’s salt marshes may be underwater by 2100. The species is listed as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List.

Industry observers note that the team, led by Garrett Maggio, a Ph.D. candidate at East Carolina University, collected mudsnails at 29 locations between April and October in 2022, 2023 and 2024.

They found the fluke at 23 of them, including new spots on Cape Cod and in Florida that push its known range farther north and south.

Out of 4,293 snails picked haphazardly and dissected, only six carried the fluke inside their bodies. But 553 had cysts. At one marsh in St. Augustine, Florida, cysts showed up on about 74 percent of the snails.

Sources indicate that the researchers also examined 38 terrapins from southern New Jersey, all females killed by cars, through a partnership with The Wetlands Institute in Stone Harbor. Seventeen of them, about 45 percent, carried adult flukes, between one and seven per turtle.

It has been revealed that some cysts turned out to be pink instead of pearly. They were first spotted in North Carolina in 2023 and later in Massachusetts and Newly introduced Jersey. The cause of the color is still unknown.

The scientists sequenced a section of mitochondrial DNA from 476 fluke samples and found 102 different variants. Most of them, 79, turned up at only one location.

Marshes farther apart had more different flukes. One variant was common across most northern marshes, and another was common across most southern ones.

The sharpest change came between Wilmington, North Carolina, and Charleston, South Carolina.

Grouping the marshes at that border explained about three times more of the genetic variation than grouping them at Cape Hatteras, the usual line between the northern diamondback terrapin and the Carolina terrapin.

In a recent development, the authors call the gap noteworthy. Adult female terrapins, the most mobile group, have been found to travel no more than about 5.3 miles (8.5 kilometers). Since the fluke only mates inside terrapins, the result raises questions about where the two subspecies really meet.

“Our findings show that this parasite may provide an important window into the ecology of diamondback terrapins,” mentioned Michael McCoy, senior author and a research professor at FAU Harbor Branch Oceanographic Institute.

The terrapin subspecies were first described from their body shape, before genetic tools were common.

Studies of terrapin DNA since then have given conflicting answers about how far the turtles move, and one study found gene flow most likely driven by people moving terrapins in the past.

Industry observers note that the authors stress that the fluke results are a starting point. They used a single genetic marker that is passed down only through the mother. A direct comparison between fluke DNA and terrapin DNA is still needed to prove the parasite truly mirrors its host.

“Rather than relying exclusively on direct observations of terrapins, we can investigate the organisms that depend on them,” McCoy noted.

Parasites make up nearly half of known biodiversity, yet they are rarely included in conservation aims. When a host declines, its parasites can vanish with it, as happened to most of the parasites once carried by New Zealand’s kākāpō.

The authors argue that the terrapin fluke deserves protection alongside its host. They add that the fluke’s wide range is evidence that terrapins are still present along much of the Atlantic coast, despite the threats they face.

The information was obtained from the study published in Ecology and Evolution and from Florida Atlantic University.

In 1980, an 8-year-old found $5,800 of D.B. Cooper’s ransom on a Columbia River sand bar, but nearly 55 years after the hijacking, the case is still unsolved

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1121 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that the FBI called the bills the only physical evidence from after D.B.
  • It has been revealed that in 1980, an eight-year-old boy named Brian Ingram was on a sand bar along the Columbia River when he found a rotting package full of $20 bills.
  • The serial numbers matched money the FBI had been looking for since 1971: part of the $200,000 ransom paid to the hijacker known as D.B.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the FBI called the bills the only physical evidence from after D.B. Cooper jumped. A paleontologist later tested the river, and in 2016 the FBI redirected the case's resources.

It has been revealed that in 1980, an eight-year-old boy named Brian Ingram was on a sand bar along the Columbia River when he found a rotting package full of $20 bills. There was $5,800 in all.

The serial numbers matched money the FBI had been looking for since 1971: part of the $200,000 ransom paid to the hijacker known as D.B. Cooper. Cooper had parachuted from a plane into the night nine years earlier.

In 2009, the FBI called that money the only physical evidence in the case from after Cooper jumped. November 24, 2026, marks 55 years since the hijacking, and the man behind it remains, in the FBI’s words, a “still-unknown individual.”.

In a recent development, on the afternoon of November 24, 1971, the day before Thanksgiving, a quiet man who called himself Dan Cooper walked up to the Northwest Orient Airlines counter in Portland, Oregon. He paid cash for a one-way ticket on Flight 305 to Seattle.

He looked to be in his mid-40s and wore a business suit, a white shirt and a black tie. While the plane waited to take off, he ordered a bourbon and soda.

Recent findings suggest that A little after 3 p.m., he handed a flight attendant a note saying he had a bomb in his briefcase. He opened the case just long enough to show her a mass of wires and red sticks. His demands were four parachutes and $200,000 in $20 bills.

In Seattle, Cooper let the 36 passengers go in exchange for the money and the parachutes. He kept several crew members on board and ordered the pilots to fly toward Mexico City.

Sources indicate that somewhere between Seattle and Reno, a little after 8 p.m., Cooper jumped out of the back of the plane with the ransom money. The pilots landed safely, but Cooper had disappeared into the night. His fate, the FBI says, “remains a mystery to this day.”.

According to recent reports, it was a cold November night with driving wind and rain, the FBI says, and he jumped somewhere between southern Washington and just north of Portland. Cloud cover at 5,000 feet meant there was no view of the ground.

Investigators first thought he was an experienced skydiver, perhaps a paratrooper, but later concluded he was not.

“No experienced parachutist would have jumped in the pitch-black night, in the rain, with a 200-mile-an-hour wind in his face, wearing loafers and a trench coat,” Larry Carr, the FBI’s Seattle case agent at the time, said in 2007.

It has been revealed that cooper had asked for four parachutes and jumped with two. One of them, a reserve chute, was meant for training and had been sewn shut, something an experienced skydiver would have checked, according to Carr. His parachute could not be steered, either.

All of this has led many FBI agents to doubt that Cooper survived the jump, though no one knows for sure. The bureau states the bills found in 1980 gave that theory “an added boost.” Only a small part of the $200,000 has ever surfaced, the FBI wrote in 2007.

The money also raised a question that is still open. Had the package been buried on that sand bar soon after the jump, or had it washed down the river over time?

In 2007, Carr suggested that science might help. “Maybe a hydrologist can use the latest technology to trace the $5,800 in ransom money found in 1980 to where Cooper landed upstream,” he mentioned.

In a recent development, in 2009, the FBI described how a group of volunteers had taken up that challenge. It was led by Tom Kaye, a paleontologist who usually searched for dinosaur bones in the Wyoming desert, and included a scientific illustrator and a metallurgist. Brian Ingram helped them too.

It has been revealed that the team ran soil, water and other experiments on the Columbia River and some of its tributaries. Using satellite maps and GPS, Kaye hoped to pinpoint exactly where Ingram had found the money.

One set of experiments, with a stack of bills on fishing line, was meant to help work out whether the money floated there over time or was buried there shortly after the jump.

Kaye also wanted to use an electron microscope to see whether pollen on Cooper’s tie came from a specific region of the country.

“After 37 years, we’re trying to use science to narrow all the possibilities,” he remarked. The bureau’s 2009 article described the work but did not report any conclusions.

Science has helped rule people out. Cooper took off his black J.C. Penney tie before he jumped, and in 2001 the FBI lifted a DNA sample from it.

According to recent reports, that sample ruled out Duane Weber, a man who had claimed on his deathbed to be the hijacker. DNA tools have since helped investigators crack other cold cases.

Recent findings suggest that the FBI called the investigation NORJAK, for Northwest hijacking. Agents interviewed hundreds of people and tracked leads across the country. By the fifth anniversary of the hijacking, they had considered more than 800 suspects and eliminated all but about two dozen.

Industry observers note that even the name is uncertain. The “D.B.” was apparently a press mistake, the FBI notes. Agents did question a man with those initials, but he was not the hijacker.

Sources indicate that carr thought the hijacker may have borrowed the name Dan Cooper from a French comic book series that was popular at the time. Its hero was a test pilot, and the cover of one episode published near the date of the hijacking demonstrated him parachuting.

In a recent development, on July 8, 2016, after 45 years, the FBI redirected the resources assigned to the case to other priorities. The evidence is being preserved for historical purposes at FBI headquarters in Washington, D.C.

Who Cooper was, whether he survived and what happened to the rest of the money are still unknown. The money a child found on a Columbia River sand bar in 1980 remains the only trace of Cooper the FBI has described from after the jump.

Industry observers note that the information was obtained from the FBI’s history page D.B. Cooper Hijacking, the FBI Seattle field office’s July 12, 2016, revision on the investigation, and the FBI stories D.B. Cooper Redux (2007) and In Search of D.B. Cooper (2009).

Tech Report: Scientists Found a Mushroom That Shouldn’t Exist: It Makes Psychedelics and Deadly Toxins

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, magic mushrooms get their magic from psilocybin and psilocin, psychedelic compounds that warp reality and open portals to other realms.
  • According to recent reports, galerina indica looks unassuming.
  • “Although the effects of psiloids and amatoxins in humans are well documented, their natural roles in the environment remain unresolved, with anti-fungivore defense being the leading hypothesis for both compound classes,” Smith and Kunik, who discovered both substances occurring in this species through mass spectrometry, stated in a study recently published in Current Biology.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, magic mushrooms get their magic from psilocybin and psilocin, psychedelic compounds that warp reality and open portals to other realms. They have also been used by Indigenous Mesoamerican and South American peoples for centuries to induce visions. Though it was once thought that mushrooms were either magic or poisonous, there is one newly discovered species that, because of a bizarre turn in evolution, produces both psilocybin and lethal amatoxins, possibly as a defense against being eaten. That’s one trip you never want to take.

According to recent reports, galerina indica looks unassuming. Growing on rotting palm trunks in the humid swamps of Florida, this tiny brown mushroom has no fairytale spots or fantastical colors, so it seems like just another fungus bound to be stepped on. Under its dark cap is a darker reality. Matthew Smith of the University of Florida is the state’s official mycologist, identifying species that could be toxic and regularly consulting with Poison Control, and his team was searching for potentially lethal mushrooms when undergrad researcher Andrew Kunik noticed something strange. While documenting fungi, he found that handling G. indica turned it blue. This often occurs in psychedelic mushrooms. Further investigation found that, despite having this telltale characteristic, the mushroom Kunik had been analyzing had a more sinister kind of magic.

“Although the effects of psiloids and amatoxins in humans are well documented, their natural roles in the environment remain unresolved, with anti-fungivore defense being the leading hypothesis for both compound classes,” Smith and Kunik, who discovered both substances occurring in this species through mass spectrometry, stated in a study recently published in Current Biology.

While G. indica did contain psilocybin, it turned out that the ‘shroom also secreted deadly amatoxins. There is no other species of mushroom known for producing both of these substances, and while trippy psiloids have been shown to have possible therapeutic properties, ingesting amatoxins is fatal because these peptides inhibit the enzyme RNA polymerase from creating RNA copies of genes, which leads to organ failure. Fungi are thought to have evolved to produce amatoxins in order to ward off fungivorous creatures such as snails and nematodes. The genes behind production of both psiloids and amatoxins are usually passed down through fungi to their descendants, but the way these genes are acquired is not always so straightforward. Previous studies have suggested they can be horizontally transferred between different fungal species.

Psiloids are known to be synthesized by a cluster of collaborative genes for which evidence of horizontal gene transfer has been found. The same is suspected of amatoxin synthesis, and though there is less evidence for horizontal transfer, it probably began with a fungal donor lineage (which may not have been the same species) that has yet to be identified. Genome analysis has shown that these and other fungal attributes were acquired by genes that were transferred from one species to another growing in the same vicinity. The genus Galerina is already infamous for amatoxins that make many mushrooms within the genus so deadly. How psiloids entered the genus remains a mystery, though just one fateful transfer could have incorporated the genes for amatoxin synthesis into these mushrooms.

Recent findings suggest that what evidence does exist for the transfer of genes that produce psiloids suggests they seeped into a lineage that did not already contain amatoxins, and in a separate evolutionary event, was absorbed by a separate toxic lineage. Kunik’s discovery also revealed how unpredictable fungi can be. The blue pigmentation that is known to be a sign of a magic mushroom comes from psilocin oligomers, molecules linked together from a few repeating structural units, or monomers. Galerina indica has shown that seeing blue does not always mean a mushroom only contains psilocin or psilocybin. While the exact genes that are responsible for amatoxins in this species are still unidentified, and exactly how psiloids evolved in the Galerina genus can only be hypothesized, there is now another thing in Florida more dangerous than alligators.

Sources indicate that “G. indica brings together in a single species the biosynthetic systems associated with both ‘magic mushrooms’ and the world’s deadliest poisonous mushrooms,” Kunik and Smith said, “providing a rare natural system for studying how horizontally acquired secondary-metabolite pathways impact organismal fitness.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Archaeologists in Cerveteri, Italy, uncovered Etruscan tombs with stone thrones, red-painted walls and a decorated jar overlooked by looters.
  • Emergency work at the Monte Abatone necropolis in Cerveteri, the Etruscan city of Caere, has turned up stone thrones, walls painted red, and a nearly intact decorated jar.
  • The work was carried out by Italy’s heritage authority for the province of Viterbo and southern Etruria, the Soprintendenza Archeologia, Belle Arti e Paesaggio.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Archaeologists in Cerveteri, Italy, uncovered Etruscan tombs with stone thrones, red-painted walls and a decorated jar overlooked by looters.

Emergency work at the Monte Abatone necropolis in Cerveteri, the Etruscan city of Caere, has turned up stone thrones, walls painted red, and a nearly intact decorated jar.

The work was carried out by Italy’s heritage authority for the province of Viterbo and southern Etruria, the Soprintendenza Archeologia, Belle Arti e Paesaggio. Some of the tombs had collapsed or become unstable.

According to recent reports, clandestine diggers had entered these tombs before the archaeologists arrived. They left the jar behind.

Industry observers note that the collapses and instability meant the tombs had to be investigated, documented and secured. The team cleared the entrances and, as a precaution, removed the fill that had built up inside.

The chambers were dug into tuff, a soft volcanic rock. Excavators have also found places on the hill where blocks of tuff were quarried in several stages.

During a 2019 excavation, a team including the University of Bonn documented a Monte Abatone tomb whose ceiling had partly fallen in along a crack.

The researchers linked such cracks to movements of the tuff layer over a less stable layer of clay. The Soprintendenza has not mentioned what caused the latest collapses, or when they occurred.

One of the chambers still keeps much of its original vaulted ceiling.

In another Etruscan chamber tomb, the funerary furniture was carved directly out of the tuff, including thrones.

A third chamber has extensive red painted decoration on its walls.

Sources indicate that similar furnishings are known from earlier work at Monte Abatone. In 2019, years before the emergency repairs, excavators recorded kline-type death beds, shaped like couches, and narrower benches lining the walls of another chamber.

Sources indicate that cerveteri’s larger Banditaccia necropolis and the Monterozzi necropolis at Tarquinia together form a UNESCO World Heritage property. At Banditaccia, thousands of tombs are laid out in a city-like blueprint, with streets and small squares.

The most complete find is an olla stamnoide, a jar shaped like a stamnos. It is almost intact. Its surface carries incised figures of animals, with some details picked out in red paint.

In a recent development, the jar will be cleaned and restored, then put on public display. No date or venue for the display has been announced.

The earlier clandestine digging compromised the original context of the burials. Some materials survived it and were recovered.

It has been revealed that looters have missed objects at Monte Abatone before. In the 2019 excavation, Tomb 642 showed signs of their digging, yet it still held a large pithos, a bucchero drinking set, Ionian bowls and Corinthian ointment jars.

Monte Abatone lies immediately south of the ancient city. It flourished in the seventh and sixth centuries BCE, according to a 2022 report on Monte Abatone.

Industry observers note that in the 1950s and 1960s, surveys and excavations explored 641 tombs there. That work was carried out on behalf of the heritage authority in response to heavy looting.

Burial types at the site include simple trench graves, chamber tombs and tombs under burial mounds, among them the Campana Tumulus.

That great mound dates to the middle of the Orientalizing period and had not been surveyed since the first half of the 19th century.

Older finds show that burials there continued from the late eighth century BCE into the Hellenistic period and the early Roman Empire.

In a recent development, researchers also examined the area west and north of the Campana Tumulus. It held tombs of the sixth to third centuries BCE, excavated in the past and partly backfilled, and funerary terraces facing the city.

It has been revealed that A research project on Monte Abatone began in the early 1990s. After a newly introduced project was set up in 2017, a group of Italian and German universities ran excavation campaigns at the site from 2018 to 2021.

Ground-penetrating radar was used across an area of about 7.4 acres (3 hectares) east of the Campana Tumulus. An earlier geophysical test had revealed a densely packed cluster of tombs.

A 2021 trial excavation opened about 13,500 square feet (1,250 square meters) south of the great tumulus. It exposed tombs with small mounds, up to about 36 feet (11 meters) across, set in two roughly parallel rows and all facing northwest.

Excavations on the south side also uncovered what the team describes as a “possible ‘family’ cluster of tombs,” used from the early Orientalizing period into the Archaic period.

“This suggests the existence of a planning by some form of ‘urban’ authority,” the authors of the 2022 report wrote about the rows of mounds.

In a recent development, laser scanners recorded the site in fine detail, producing a combined model of about 4.3 billion points, roughly 1.2 billion of them for the Campana Tumulus alone. A drone survey added a photogrammetric model of the plateau.

The information was obtained from the Soprintendenza for the province of Viterbo and southern Etruria.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that this is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

Dor Minzer remembers sitting in an undergraduate computation class at Tel Aviv University. He was intrigued by his professor and soon found himself pulled into a new world: the mystifying intersection of math and computation, first laid out by Alan Turing during World War II. Working with the professor, Minzer became deeply interested in the limitations of what computers can and can’t do.

Industry observers note that “My part is actually to prove not only do I not know how to do it, but I can prove that it’s impossible,” Minzer claims. “You have to really be curious.”.

According to recent reports, minzer’s hard work has paid off. In 2018, he proved a theoretical computer science problem called the 2-to-2 games conjecture. It asks whether computers can efficiently distinguish games where almost all rules can be satisfied from those where almost none can be satisfied, when the rules have a strict structure.

In September, Minzer and his two graduate students at MIT posted a 95-page milestone paper on the unique games conjecture, which builds off the 2-to-2 conjecture. The paper wasn’t quite ready, but they published to get ahead of a press release from OpenAI, describing its proof for the same problem, slated for only days later. It’s a situation that many mathematicians have found themselves in this year as AI companies flood the field with findings at lightning speed.

In a recent development, minzer says it’s critical to remember that math, and all the research and contemplation behind it, is very human. “It’s a human activity,” he says. “Research is sort of a living organism, a living body.”.

Recent findings suggest that minzer teaches his own students now. Some days, he talks to his class and gets the sense that nobody is paying attention. But other days, he gets a few students that participate. They have ideas, they’re excited, and they remind him of his own days as a graduate student.

Sources indicate that “I feel like now I feel like I’m passing the torch,” he says. “Before you have a Ph.D. adviser, you’re like a upcoming person in a dark room. There are infinite places to go. Your Ph.D. adviser is the person that holds your hand and says, ‘Okay, let’s walk here.’”.

#123851. Wild baboons seem to initiative breakfast around a favorite fruit

Wild baboons seem to initiative breakfast around a favorite fruit

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1380 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Wild baboons stopped visiting their favorite fruit trees after a fire destroyed the crop, suggesting flexible food planning.
  • Wild Guinea baboons in West Africa travel to the same area each year to feed on a favored fruit.
  • Sources indicate that the fire reached the area just as the fruit was beginning to ripen on the trees.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Wild baboons stopped visiting their favorite fruit trees after a fire destroyed the crop, suggesting flexible food planning.

Wild Guinea baboons in West Africa travel to the same area each year to feed on a favored fruit. In 2019, this annual pattern was disrupted by a fire that swept through the feeding grounds.

Sources indicate that the fire reached the area just as the fruit was beginning to ripen on the trees. Only a single visit to the fruit trees was recorded during February of that year.

The baboons resumed their usual visits the following year, when ripe Natal oranges were available again.

Sources indicate that these observations suggest that the animals do more than simply recall where and when food can be found. Their foraging plans also appear to be revised when a familiar food source is lost.

The study was led by Lisa Ohrndorf of the German Primate Center in Göttingen, Germany.

“The year of the fire gave us a unique opportunity: We were able to observe how the animals react when a normally reliable food source suddenly becomes unavailable during their usual season,” said Ohrndorf.

In a recent development, her co-authors were Roger Mundry, Dietmar Zinner and Julia Fischer. All three are affiliated with the center and with the University of Göttingen.

The baboons inhabit Niokolo-Koba National Park in southeastern Senegal, where several groups have been followed by researchers since 2007.

Earlier work carried out at the same center had shown that these baboons share meat with close companions.

A clear preference for the Natal orange is shown by the animals during the dry season. The fruit is roughly the size of a common orange and is protected by a hard outer shell.

Inside the shell the seeds are embedded in a layer of soft pulp that is eaten by the baboons.

In a recent development, natal oranges ripen between January and March and reach their greatest abundance in February. Data from recent years indicate that nearly a fifth of February feeding time was devoted to this fruit.

Very few other plants in the park are known to produce fleshy fruit during the dry season. The long journey to the Natal orange trees is therefore likely to be well rewarded.

Most of the Natal orange trees are found in the northern parts of the home ranges of the baboons.

These trees cannot be seen from the riverside forest in which the animals usually spend the night.

In 2023 a series of evenly spaced survey routes was walked by the researchers through the area. A total of 5,847 Natal orange trees was counted along these routes.

The densest stand found in this survey was then used as the target area for the analysis of baboon movements.

According to recent reports, fires are a regular feature of the park and are recorded in every dry season. They normally burn between mid-December and early January and mainly consume the tall grass left after the rains.

The fires of 2019 were unusual because they arrived much later than in most years.

Satellite records indicate that most of the target area burned within a few days at the end of January. By that point the Natal oranges had already begun to ripen.

Recent findings suggest that nearly all of the ripe fruit was destroyed by the heat of the fire. The trees themselves suffered little lasting damage and plant growth in the following rainy season was close to normal.

According to recent reports, nine years of observation records for seven baboon groups were examined by the team. Each group contained an average of 29 animals.

The baboons were observed on 22 days in February 2019 but entered the target area on only one of them. In other years between eight and 29 visits were recorded in February with an average of about 16.

Sources indicate that during the fire year the baboons were seen feeding on the fruit of fan palms. The fruit of a shrubby tree growing in other parts of their range was also eaten.

The baboons visited the area four times in March 2019, at the low end of the range of four to 22 visits recorded in other years.

The baboons may have returned in March to feed on fruit from taller trees, where it hangs higher and is less exposed to the heat of a fire.

By 2020 the Natal oranges had recovered and the usual pattern of visits to the area had resumed.

The researchers also analyzed 2,922 GPS tracks that had been collected over a period of nine years.

Of those tracks, 530 showed a group entering the area where the fruit trees grow.

When Natal oranges were in season the baboons were found to follow more direct routes to the trees. Their average travel speed on these trips was also about 14% higher than at other times of year.

According to recent reports, the distance involved in these trips was considerable. From the known sleeping sites the trees lay roughly 1.4 miles (2.2 kilometers) away in a straight line.

Baboons are generally slow to leave their sleeping trees in the morning. More than an hour commonly passes between sunrise and their departure.

On trips to the feeding area, the baboons left their sleeping sites about 40 minutes earlier when the fruit was in season.

Cold weather normally delays departure because the animals tend to sun themselves before setting off.

Industry observers note that mornings in the fruit season were in fact colder on average. Since the baboons still left earlier, warmer temperatures cannot account for the change.

It has been revealed that in studies of animal learning a distinction is drawn between habitual behavior and behavior driven by an expected reward. A habit may persist for some time after the associated reward is no longer available.

It has been revealed that the direct and rapid trips to the trees could in principle have reflected nothing more than a fixed yearly routine. The response of the baboons to the fire argues against that interpretation.

It has been revealed that if the visits had been governed by habit alone the empty trees would probably have continued to be visited. The baboons instead shifted their foraging to food sources located in other parts of their range.

The results suggest that the value of a journey is assessed by these baboons before the journey is undertaken.

Comparable behavior has been described in several other primates. Chacma baboons have been observed leaving their sleeping sites early in order to reach fig trees. Female chimpanzees leave their nests earlier when a preferred fruit is located far away.

Memory for food locations is not restricted to primates. Small birds such as chickadees are able to recall where large numbers of their food stores were hidden.

According to recent reports, responses to fire are also known to vary widely among animals. Some deer return to burned ground within days while certain lizards detect smoke and move away before the flames arrive.

Industry observers note that the late fire occurred only once during the study period. Visit numbers could therefore be compared across years but full statistical testing of the fire year was not possible.

GPS positions were recorded at 30-minute intervals during follows that usually ended around 1 p.m. Some movement was missed as a result and the actual routes were probably longer and less direct.

The means by which the baboons navigate through their home range also remains unclear. Repeated use of the same trails and roads and stream crossings points to a reliance on learned routes.

A further open question concerns the way in which the baboons recognize that the Natal oranges are ready to eat.

Day length and temperature or the appearance of other seasonal foods may serve as cues for the animals. These possibilities were not tested in the present study.

The study offers a closer look at the way wild baboons make decisions about where to search for food.

Knowledge of where food grows is clearly useful but knowing when to stop searching may be equally crucial.

The full study was published in the journal Animal Cognition.

Stomach problems in autistic children raise fresh questions about gut bacteria

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1283 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A study found that autistic children with more severe digestive symptoms tended to have more difficulty picking up on social cues.
  • Children with autism often have stomach problems.
  • Little evidence for that explanation was found in a new study.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A study found that autistic children with more severe digestive symptoms tended to have more difficulty picking up on social cues.

Children with autism often have stomach problems. What causes them, however, is still up for debate. Some scientists believe the lining of the gut becomes damaged or inflamed.

Little evidence for that explanation was found in a new study.

Autistic children with more severe digestive symptoms tended to have more difficulty picking up on social cues, according to parent questionnaires.

The researchers also found links between certain gut bacteria and digestive symptoms.

According to recent reports, the study was led by J. Marc Rhoads. He is professor and chief of the Division of Gastroenterology, Hepatology, and Nutrition at McGovern Medical School at UTHealth Houston.

Recent findings suggest that many children with autism are unable to explain where they feel pain. In such cases a change in behavior may be the first sign of a problem.

“Families may notice increased irritability, repetitive behaviors, or self-injurious behaviors when a child is experiencing gastrointestinal concerns such as gas, constipation, or diarrhea,” Rhoads stated.

“For children who are nonverbal, these behaviors may be one of the few ways they can communicate discomfort.”.

About one in 31 American eight-year-olds had been identified with autism in 2022. This estimate was published by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

Significant digestive problems have been reported in 31% to 84% of people with autism in earlier studies.

It has been revealed that the researchers examined 72 children with autism who were between four and 16 years of age. All of the children had been enrolled in a probiotic trial. Their data were collected between 2016 and 2023.

Boys made up about 78% of the group and roughly a quarter of the children did not speak. Children with known digestive, liver or kidney diseases were excluded from the study. Those who had recently taken antibiotics or probiotics were also left out.

It has been revealed that several symptoms were assessed by the team. These included constipation, gas, stomach pain, unusually smelly stools and waking up at night.

Recent findings suggest that A score of seven or more on a 17-point scale was taken to indicate significant digestive problems. About 63% of the children were placed in this group.

Parents were also asked to complete a questionnaire about the social behavior of their children. Higher scores on this questionnaire reflected more pronounced autism traits.

Industry observers note that higher scores were generally seen in children with worse stomach problems. The connection was not particularly strong but it reached statistical significance.

It has been revealed that the clearest difference was observed in social awareness. This area covers abilities such as noticing the facial expressions, feelings or actions of another person.

Children with significant digestive problems scored about 7.5 points higher in this area. Their scores were compared with those of children who had milder symptoms.

The cells that line the intestines are packed closely together. The spaces between them are sealed by specialized proteins.

Substances from inside the gut may pass into the bloodstream if these seals are weakened. Inflammation could then be triggered in the body. This process is commonly described as a leaky gut.

In a recent development, blood samples were tested for two proteins associated with these seals. Another blood protein linked to intestinal inflammation was measured as well. Stool samples were also analyzed for calprotectin, a protein routinely used by doctors to detect gut inflammation.

Most of the results fell within the normal range. Elevated calprotectin was detected in only two children and neither of them had significant digestive symptoms.

“Biomarkers of intestinal inflammation and gut permeability remained within normal ranges and were not associated with gastrointestinal symptom severity or autism symptom severity,” Rhoads stated.

Children with worse stomach problems therefore did not show more signs of inflammation or a leaky gut on these tests.

According to recent reports, mixed results have been produced by earlier research. High calprotectin levels were found in up to a third of autistic children in some studies. No significant difference was found in a more recent review.

The bacterial findings proved to be more revealing than the blood tests.

Recent findings suggest that additional stool samples were obtained from Texas Children’s Microbiome Center. This allowed the analysis to be expanded to 135 children. The group included children with autism, their siblings and unrelated children without autism.

It has been revealed that fewer types of gut bacteria were present in children with autism than in their siblings. A similar difference was seen when they were compared with unrelated children. However, this second result may have arisen by chance.

The bacterial communities of children with autism also resembled one another more closely. Greater variety was observed among the other children.

In a recent development, two groups of bacteria were more abundant in autistic children with significant digestive problems. One of these groups is known as Ruminococcus.

Industry observers note that children with higher levels of these bacteria reported more gas and stronger-smelling stools. Night waking was also more frequent in these children. Their overall digestive symptom scores were higher as well.

It has been revealed that ruminococcus feeds on the mucus that protects the intestinal wall. Higher levels of this bacterium in one-year-olds were linked to greater social difficulties at age three in an earlier study.

According to recent reports, another bacterial group called Sarcina was associated with gas, stomach pain, diarrhea and night waking. The researchers noted that Sarcina had not been linked to autism in previous studies.

The study captured a snapshot of digestive symptoms, gut bacteria and behavior.

Recent findings suggest that the children were examined at a single point in time. It was therefore not possible to tell which change came first.

Gut bacteria may cause stomach problems, or digestive problems may alter the bacterial population.

Diet could also play a part in this relationship. Many children with autism prefer a limited range of foods. The bacteria living in the intestines are strongly influenced by what a person eats.

In a recent development, the study also had a few other limitations. Blood was not collected from healthy children for ethical reasons. Results were compared with established normal ranges instead.

Industry observers note that children with known digestive diseases were excluded by the team. Some of the analyses did not account for other factors that might have influenced the findings.

In a recent development, children could be followed over several years in future studies. Such work may show whether changes in gut bacteria occur before digestive or behavioral changes.

Rhoads believes that everyday habits deserve more attention.

“This study highlights the importance of supporting a healthy gut microbiome in children with autism,” Rhoads remarked.

“A varied diet rich in fruits, vegetables, and whole grains, along with healthy toileting habits, may help improve both gastrointestinal health and behavior.”.

“Our team has also found promising results with probiotic treatment.”.

Industry observers note that the results of the probiotic trial have not yet been published. Scientists are still working to determine which probiotic supplements are helpful and under what conditions.

The most useful lesson for parents may concern the recognition of discomfort rather than bacteria.

A child may suddenly become irritable, sleep poorly or show more repetitive behaviors. Such changes may be caused by something as ordinary as constipation or stomach pain.

Many children are unable to put this discomfort into words. Behavior may be one of the ways in which they ask for help.

The study is published in the journal Pediatric Research.

This Guy Found a Security Camera’s Exact Location Using Only the Sound of Two Planes

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Recent findings suggest that mind you, this audio doesn’t have any useful hints.
  • To start his journey toward pinpointing the location of this video, with the only limitation being it was filmed somewhere in the continental U.S., the YouTuber first turned to Automatic Dependent Surveillance–Broadcast data, or ADS-B, provided by aircraft equipment that constantly report speed, velocity, and altitude.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that geoguessr is a widely popular online geography game where players glimpse one still frame from Google Street View and then attempt to pinpoint the exact location on a world map. Many things can be helpful hints—the design of road signs, the format of license plates, specific road markings as well as surrounding trees and landscapes. However, a YouTuber named colsto took this idea to a whole new level by geolocating an incredibly grainy video by just its captured audio.

Recent findings suggest that mind you, this audio doesn’t have any useful hints. No one nearby is talking about this “da Bears” game with a thick Chicago accent, for example. But buried within the security camera’s spectrogram (visual display of frequencies over time) is a clue—two of them, in fact. To the uninitiated they look relatively innocuous two sloping lights roughly 920 seconds apart, but colsto recognized these lines as the Doppler effect signatures of a two planes passing overhead.

To start his journey toward pinpointing the location of this video, with the only limitation being it was filmed somewhere in the continental U.S., the YouTuber first turned to Automatic Dependent Surveillance–Broadcast data, or ADS-B, provided by aircraft equipment that constantly report speed, velocity, and altitude. Websites like Flightradar24 rely on this data to provide a real-time snapshot of on-going flights around the world. Colsto first cross-referenced this data and winnowed potential candidates by choosing parameters featuring two planes the right speed and the right distance away while still traveling within 920 seconds of each other. The results weren’t promising.

“That gave us…roughly 70,000 points,” colsto claims in the video. “Now, adding on to all that logic, the silence filter—where that point doesn’t hear another flight between the two events—drops from 70,000 to 15,000. Even with all those constraints, there is just so much land area and so many flights that 15,000 points still meet all those criteria.”.

According to recent reports, instead of going through each data point, ruling out why it doesn’t fit and refining the search parameters, colsto returned to the Doppler curves and revised one of the search’s original assumptions. These two curves didn’t represent a perfect Doppler curve because planes are constantly adjusting speed and heading, and that information—no matter how slight—is locked away within these two curves. So colsto modeled the Doppler curves to create a flight path that could then be checked against 15,000 possible points.

According to recent reports, “The Doppler curve is a function of the radial velocity of the plane with respect to the observer,” colsto indicates in the video. “The Doppler curve would change depending on the plane geometry.”.

Eventually, colsto found the exact security camera located in Oyster Bay in Long Island, New York, that captured the grainy security footage of the pixelated tree line.

Industry observers note that “I’m trying to fear monger with this video. The odds that someone can and does actually do this is pretty slim,” colsto said at the video’s conclusion. “In reality, there’s probably one hundred easier ways to find you than this.”.

That isn’t immensely reassuring.

In a recent development, darren lives in Portland, has a cat, and writes/edits about sci-fi and how our world works. You can find his previous stuff at Gizmodo and Paste if you look hard enough.

#123848. Latest Update: Plants can grow elaborate leaves, so why are most of them so simple?

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1544 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: Plants can grow elaborate leaves, so why are most of them so simple?

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1544 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A study suggests that the way leaves grow helps explain why most flowering plants have simple leaves, even though complex shapes have evolved many times.
  • Recent findings suggest that the leaves of a maple tree, a rose bush and a magnolia bear very little resemblance to one another.
  • Complex leaf shapes have arisen many times during the evolution of flowering plants.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A study suggests that the way leaves grow helps explain why most flowering plants have simple leaves, even though complex shapes have evolved many times.

Recent findings suggest that the leaves of a maple tree, a rose bush and a magnolia bear very little resemblance to one another. Deep cuts are seen in some of them. Others are made up of several small leaflets or one unbroken blade.

Complex leaf shapes have arisen many times during the evolution of flowering plants. Simple leaves have nevertheless remained by far the most common form.

A upcoming study suggests that the way leaves grow helps explain why leaves with a single blade and no deep cuts are so common.

Random changes were introduced by the researchers into a computer model that simulates a growing leaf.

No particular shape was favored in those runs but simple leaves were still produced far more often than other kinds.

The research was led by James Malone, a graduate student in the Department of Physics at the University of Oxford.

It has been revealed that he was joined by Ard Louis, a professor of theoretical physics at Oxford. Researchers in Barcelona and at Stony Brook University in Newly introduced York also took part.

“What we found is that you can largely explain which leaf shapes dominate in evolution simply by looking at how leaves develop and how mutations affect that process, without needing to invoke natural selection,” noted Malone.

“The bias towards simplicity is built into the developmental system itself.”.

For the purposes of the study, every leaf was assigned to one of four broad groups based on its outline.

An unlobed leaf consists of a single blade with no deep cuts along its edge. In a lobed leaf the blade is divided by cuts into distinct sections.

Those cuts extend much further toward the center in a dissected leaf. Separate leaflets attached to one shared stalk are what make up a compound leaf.

According to recent reports, large differences in leaf form can be found even among closely related plants. All four leaf types are represented among species of the geranium group Pelargonium.

Both lobed and unlobed leaves may even be produced on a single mulberry tree, as the authors pointed out.

In a recent development, different leaf shapes do not necessarily require different genes. Much of the variety depends on the timing and location of gene activity inside a developing leaf.

Comparable genetic processes determine whether single leaves or leaves divided into three parts are grown by strawberry plants.

For centuries, botanists have collected, pressed and dried plants for long-term storage. Such specimens are held in collections known as herbariums that now serve as a record of plant diversity.

Industry observers note that the team looked at 8,911 digital images of specimens from the Naturalis Biodiversity Center in Leiden, the Netherlands. The shape of each leaf was identified by hand.

It has been revealed that the identified shapes were then placed onto five large family trees of flowering plants. One of these trees included 9,506 species and was based on information from 353 genes.

In 2012 an earlier study of 561 plants had reported that about 76% of them carried unlobed leaves. That share rose to between 86% and nearly 89% in the much larger trees used for the newly introduced study.

The frequency of leaf shape changes during evolution was then estimated from those labeled trees. Complex leaves were found to give way to unlobed ones far more readily than unlobed leaves became complex.

Recent findings suggest that all five family trees highlighted this pattern. No disagreement was seen among the trees on the direction of any clearly established shift.

It seems natural to assume that simple leaves give plants some kind of edge over complex ones.

The shape of a leaf is known to influence the way heat and water are managed by the plant. Sunlight capture and protection from plant-eating animals may also be affected by it.

Recent findings suggest that in one experiment with paper leaves, symmetrical unlobed shapes sank the fastest. Such behavior could allow the nutrients in fallen leaves to stay closer to the parent tree.

In a recent development, when earlier research was reviewed by the authors, the evidence for selection proved much stronger for leaf size. Far weaker support was found for selection on these four broad shapes.

In many of those studies it was shown that shape changes how a leaf works. Far fewer showed that a given shape actually helps a plant survive and reproduce. Many also looked only at certain groups of plants.

“For many biological traits, such as the camera eye with its lens and retina, complexity clearly accumulates over time through natural selection,” Louis noted.

Sources indicate that “But leaf shape shows the opposite pattern. Complexity evolves – and then evolution frequently abandons it.”.

A different explanation was therefore explored using a model built by Adam Runions and colleagues in 2017.

Leaf growth in this model is driven by the veins and edge along with chemical signals acting on that edge.

Before the main experiment began the model was compared with results that had been obtained in real plants.

Earlier work on thale cress and hairy bittercress had shown that compound leaves need two genes active together.

Lobes alone were formed in thale cress when only one of those two genes was switched on.

The model behaved in the same way once its two most comparable settings had been adjusted.

Twenty of the 25 tested combinations of those settings went on to produce simple unlobed leaves.

The main experiment was started from 48 virtual leaves that represented all four shapes between them.

Each setting in turn received a small random change and this went on for 320 steps. Five runs were made from every starting leaf and 76,800 virtual leaves came out of the experiment.

Rejection was limited to physically unrealistic leaves such as those in which veins filled too little of the blade.

No leaf was rewarded for its shape and yet about three-quarters of the virtual leaves were found to be unlobed.

Within the margins of error the model’s rates of change toward simple shapes matched those of the family trees.

The model’s settings can be imagined as a long list of instructions for growing one leaf.

Random edits to that list would mostly still end in a leaf with a simple outline.

A far more specific combination of settings is needed to produce a more elaborate leaf, as the researchers found.

The settings for unlobed leaves were grouped into only three separate regions within the model.

Lobed leaves by contrast were spread over 131 regions while dissected leaves occupied 96 and compound leaves 235.

Many of the small regions that gave complex leaves were located inside the much larger region that gave simple ones.

The arrangement can be compared to a mostly green map on which hundreds of tiny blue patches have been scattered.

A few random steps taken from a blue patch would often lead a walker onto green ground.

Someone who started out in the green area might travel a long way before reaching any blue at all. Leaf development appears to work in a comparable way according to the study’s results.

Complex leaves are easily turned into simple ones by random genetic change while the opposite outcome is less likely.

Switches from one complex shape to another such as from lobed to compound were handled less well by the model.

The real family trees were also more likely to disagree with one another about these particular changes.

The authors suggested that natural selection may have had a larger influence on those shifts. It is also possible that some of the finer details of complex leaf growth are not captured by the model.

Closed net-like vein patterns cannot be recreated by it and the parallel veins common in grasses are also absent.

Much of what is known about leaf growth has been learned from a handful of laboratory plants.

Every group of flowering plants may therefore not be represented equally well by a single model.

The small teeth found along the edges of some leaves were not included in the analysis. Hand classification of thousands of herbarium images also put a limit on the amount of usable data.

Whether similar patterns exist elsewhere in nature is the question the researchers hope to answer next.

Tree and root shapes will be examined next along with tooth complexity and the fins of African cichlid fish.

“By continuing this approach – combining large-scale analysis of evolutionary trees with computer simulations – we will gain a much greater understanding of how the complexity of a trait evolves over time across different kingdoms of life,” stated Louis.

Folded RNA molecules and grouped proteins had already shown a similar preference for simple forms in earlier work.

Evolution can certainly produce complicated structures but greater complexity is not always the direction it takes.

One reason simple leaves may be so common is that plants have more ways to grow them.

The full study was published in the journal eLife.

Trump says no Iran deal needed after conflict drove GOP’s midterm losses

💡 Key Takeaways

  • President Donald Trump on Thursday shut down his administration’s on-again-off-again talks with Iran, saying he would not seek a deal to formally end the nine-month-old conflict with Tehran.
  • The possible end of the pursuit of a diplomatic solution came nine days after Trump and congressional Republicans suffered massive losses in the midterm elections.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that president Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance salute during a Wednesday ceremony at Arlington National Cemetery in honor of Veterans Day. (Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images).

President Donald Trump on Thursday shut down his administration’s on-again-off-again talks with Iran, saying he would not seek a deal to formally end the nine-month-old conflict with Tehran.

The possible end of the pursuit of a diplomatic solution came nine days after Trump and congressional Republicans suffered massive losses in the midterm elections. House Democrats will have more than 250 seats come January, and Senate Democrats will have at least 55 seats in the Senate — with Alaska’s competitive race still uncalled.

Polls leading up to Election Day and since have shown that a majority of voters, and a sizeable chunk of Trump’s Republican base, felt the Iran conflict was a mistake.

Vice President JD Vance penned a lengthy social media post the day after the election, blaming, in large part, the Iran war for the coast-to-coast Democratic victories. Some GOP lawmakers have also called for an end to the conflict, which drove up fuel and other commodity prices.

"The reason we lost is the war," Vance wrote the morning after the GOP wipeout. "The president himself said so last night.".

Trump has mentioned that he agrees with Vance’s assessment but that if he had to decide again whether to join Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in striking Iranian targets, he would reach the same conclusion. On Monday, he told reporters that the Iran war "militarily is effectively over.".

Vance had been Trump’s designated top negotiator in the talks with Iran’s remaining leaders, but the president stated Thursday on social media that he had ordered his second-in-command to instead “focus his complete and total attention on the Massive Corruption and Crime taking place in Democrat run Cities and States throughout the U.S.”.

According to recent reports, “We don’t need a deal with Iran. Those days have long since passed,” he added. “We’ve got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we’ve got their Strait!".

The situation along the Strait of Hormuz remains contested and dangerous for commercial vessels, including ones that deliver a large amount of the world’s oil products. Iranian officials contend that they control most of the key waterway.

Trump, Vance and other administration officials have stated in recent weeks that they were open to continuing talks with Iran, while criticizing Tehran's negotiating tactics. Last week, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who also is Trump’s national security adviser, told reporters that Iran's latest demands were unreasonable.

Trump’s announcement Thursday could represent his latest way to try assuaging GOP voters, including members of his “Make America Great Again” base. A Reuters/Ipsos poll conducted after the midterms and released Tuesday showed that a majority of Republicans (51 percent) want Congress to pass legislation that would end the Iran conflict. Overall, 71 percent of Americans would support such a bill, the survey found.

The conflict was front-and-center during the midterms campaign.

Recent findings suggest that republican former Rep. Mike Rogers, who lost the Senate race in Michigan to Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, called for the Iran conflict to end "promptly.".

According to recent reports, “Michigan families are struggling with the price of everyday life. Groceries cost too much. We have to bring prices down," Rogers said in one campaign ad.

On Capitol Hill, GOP lawmakers have tried giving Trump cover, while raising some concerns about high gas prices and questioning whether the president and his team have a viable exit strategy.

As the midterms campaign hit the homestretch in late September, two Iowa Republicans in tight races, Reps. Zach Nunn and Mariannette Miller-Meeks, voted with Democrats on a measure to end the conflict.

“With the negotiating window closed, sustained combat operations now require congressional authorization,” Nunn, an Air Force veteran, wrote on social media. “I will not support another open-ended war.”.

Nunn and Miller-Meeks both lost their seats last week, despite breaking with the president over the war.

Trump’s declaration this week of a military end to the Iran war came more than seven years after he offered some foreshadowing during a June 25, 2019, exchange with this CQ Roll Call reporter in the Oval Office.

According to recent reports, asked that day what his exit strategy would be if war ever broke out with Iran, he said: “You’re not going to need an exit strategy. I don’t do exit strategies.”.
